topic: Faraday cage and lightning in cars
prompt: Explain why you are safe inside a metal car during a lightning storm, gently correcting the common belief that the rubber tyres are what protect you.
Explain Schrödinger's cat thought experiment and why Schrödinger originally meant it as a mockery of quantum superposition rather than a serious description of reality.
Explain the two envelopes paradox, in which a seemingly airtight expected-value argument tells you to keep swapping your envelope forever, and pinpoint where the reasoning quietly goes wrong.

Explain the ancient problem of universals by asking what a ripe tomato, a fire engine and a drop of blood share when we call them all red, and whether redness exists over and above the red things themselves.

Narrate the scene in Paris in August 1900 when David Hilbert stood before the International Congress of Mathematicians and laid out the unsolved problems he believed would shape the coming century, capturing his conviction that every mathematical question could be answered.

topic: Walking the moai of Rapa Nui
prompt: Write a story set on Rapa Nui in which villagers use ropes to rock a towering moai from side to side, 'walking' the statue upright across the island toward its platform by the sea.

topic: grandfather paradox and past time travel
prompt: Argue whether the grandfather paradox proves that travel into the past is impossible, or merely that a self-consistent universe would always find a way to stop you from changing history.
Describe what it would be like to walk as a Nabataean caravan trader through the narrow, twisting Siq canyon and catch your first glimpse of Petra's Treasury glowing rose-red in the living rock.
Explain Brouwer's fixed-point theorem through the image of gently stirring a cup of coffee, showing why at least one point of the liquid must end up exactly where it began.

Describe the moment Henri Poincaré, setting his foot on the step of a bus at Coutances, suddenly realized that the functions he had been struggling with were tied to non-Euclidean geometry, and reflect on the role of the unconscious in mathematical discovery.

topic: John Snow and the Broad Street pump
prompt: Explain how John Snow used a map of cholera deaths in 1854 London to trace an outbreak to a single water pump on Broad Street, laying a foundation for modern epidemiology.

Write an evocative passage about the Boötes Void, a region of space hundreds of millions of light-years across that contains astonishingly few galaxies, imagining the night sky from a planet at its center.

Explain earthshine, the faint ghostly glow on the dark part of a crescent moon that Leonardo da Vinci correctly attributed to sunlight bouncing off the Earth, and dwell on the idea that we are seeing our own planet's reflected light.

topic: retired COBOL programmer recalled to legacy system
prompt: Write a short story about a retired COBOL programmer called back to rescue a decades-old government system that no one still working understands, who finds traces of her younger self in the comments she once left in it.

Describe what it would be like to live inside Jeremy Bentham's panopticon, a circular prison where a central tower might be watching you at any moment, and how the mere possibility of being seen becomes a guard inside your own head.
Explain Fermat's principle of least time, using the analogy of a lifeguard choosing the fastest path across sand and water to reach a swimmer, to show why light bends when it enters water.
Explain the research suggesting that prairie dog alarm calls encode details about a predator, such as its species, its size and even the color of a person's shirt.
Argue whether the 'hot hand' in basketball is a cognitive illusion, as researchers claimed for decades, or a real phenomenon that a subtle statistical error had been hiding.
Explain why the 1995 discovery of 51 Pegasi b, a giant planet whipping around its star in just four days, upended astronomers' assumptions about how planetary systems are arranged.

Explain how the humble potato, carried from the Andes to Europe after 1492, fuelled population booms across the Old World, and how heavy dependence on a single crop set the stage for tragedy in Ireland.
Make a playful but serious case for whether mathematics would be clearer if we abandoned pi in favor of tau, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its radius.

Write a brief story in which an ordinary modern person finds a ring like the one in Plato's myth of Gyges, which makes its wearer invisible, and must discover whether they are honest only because they are watched.

Explain the concept of a Giffen good, the rare case in which a rise in price makes poor households buy more of a staple, as was claimed for potatoes in famine-era Ireland and later documented for rice in rural China.
Argue whether viruses should be considered living things, weighing their lack of metabolism against their ability to evolve and reproduce inside cells.
Explain why fever is not merely a symptom but an ancient defense strategy, describing how a raised body temperature helps the immune system fight infection.
Compare absolute advantage with comparative advantage, using the example of a top lawyer who types faster than her assistant yet still gains by letting the assistant do all the typing.

Describe what it would be like to stand in the path of a total solar eclipse at the moment of totality, as the air turns suddenly cold, birds fall silent and a pearly corona blooms around a perfectly black disc.

Explain the attention mechanism at the heart of transformer language models using the image of a reader whose eyes dart back across a sentence to work out what the word 'it' refers to, weighing every earlier word by its relevance.

topic: Big Mac Index and purchasing power
prompt: Explain the idea of purchasing power parity through the Big Mac Index, showing how comparing the price of the same burger across countries can hint at whether a currency is overvalued or undervalued.

Explain Ned Block's China brain thought experiment, in which the entire population of China simulates a single brain by passing signals over two-way radios, and ask whether the nation as a whole would feel anything.

Describe a single day in the life of a resident of Mohenjo-daro around 2500 BCE, moving through the carefully planned Indus Valley city of grid-like streets, covered drains, brick houses and the Great Bath.

topic: no one can make a pencil
prompt: Explain the idea behind Leonard Read's essay 'I, Pencil', that no single person on Earth knows how to make an ordinary pencil from scratch, by letting the pencil itself describe the forests, mines, factories and strangers that went into it.

topic: salmon carrying ocean nutrients into forests
prompt: Explain how spawning salmon carry nutrients from the ocean into coastal rainforests, so that trees along salmon streams contain marine nitrogen delivered by bears and eagles.

Explain the Coase theorem using the classic dispute between a cattle rancher whose herd tramples a neighboring farmer's crops, showing why cheap bargaining leads to the efficient outcome regardless of who is legally liable.
Describe the Sun's distant future as it swells into a red giant, what its bloated disk would look like from the scorched remains of Earth, and the glowing nebula it will finally leave behind.
Argue whether a space elevator, a cable stretching from Earth's equator to beyond geostationary orbit, is a realistic engineering goal or a beautiful impossibility.
Explain, with a light and humorous touch, the 'banana equivalent dose' of radiation and what it reveals about the natural radioactivity of potassium in our food and in our own bodies.
Explain, with playful examples, the Great Vowel Shift, the centuries-long upheaval in how English vowels were pronounced that left English spelling so famously out of step with its sounds.

Explain Heidegger's distinction between the ready-to-hand and the present-at-hand, using the moment a hammer breaks mid-swing and suddenly becomes a strange object rather than an extension of the hand.
Describe what daily life would feel like inside an O'Neill cylinder, a rotating space habitat where 'up' points toward the central axis and the landscape curves overhead in every direction.
Explain how the number e emerges from Jacob Bernoulli's question about compounding interest more and more frequently, in a way that makes e feel as natural and inevitable as pi.
Compare Fred Hoyle's steady-state theory of an eternal, unchanging universe with the Big Bang model, explaining what each predicted and which observations decided between them.
Write a brief story narrated by a Judean date palm seed that lay dormant for two thousand years in the ruins of Masada before scientists coaxed it into sprouting and named the sapling Methuselah.
Explain what E=mc² actually means, including the surprising consequence that a hot cup of coffee or a wound-up watch is very slightly heavier than a cold or unwound one.

Explain how deaf children brought together in Nicaraguan schools in the late 1970s and 1980s spontaneously created a new sign language, and why linguists treat its emergence as a rare window into how grammar is born.

topic: The block universe and timeless reality
prompt: Describe what it would be like to see the universe as a 'block' in which past, present and future all exist equally, so that your childhood birthday party is as real right now as this very moment.

topic: Colladon's light fountain and fibre optics
prompt: Explain how Daniel Colladon in 1842 trapped light inside a curving stream of water in his 'light fountain,' and how the same principle of total internal reflection now carries the internet through optical fibres.

topic: male moth following a pheromone plume
prompt: Describe the night flight of a male moth following an invisible plume of a female's scent across kilometers of dark countryside, detecting it a few molecules at a time.

topic: the sloth as a walking ecosystem
prompt: Write a whimsical description of a three-toed sloth as a slow-moving ecosystem, with algae greening its fur and moths living in its coat.

Describe a performance of the Mechanical Turk, the eighteenth-century chess-playing automaton in Ottoman robes that astonished European courts, from the point of view of a spectator who does not yet know a human chess master is hidden inside.
Write a lyrical description of the Pantheon in Rome on a rainy day, as light and raindrops fall through the open oculus at the crown of its ancient concrete dome onto the marble floor below.
Explain how a solar sail can propel a spacecraft using nothing but the gentle pressure of sunlight, and why such a tiny, constant push can eventually build up enormous speeds.

topic: why stars twinkle but planets don't
prompt: Explain why stars twinkle while planets usually shine with a steady light, in terms a curious child on a camping trip could follow.

Explain the pessimistic meta-induction, the argument that because so many once-successful scientific theories, like the luminiferous ether and phlogiston, turned out false, our current best theories probably will too.

Explain how Aristarchus of Samos proposed a Sun-centred universe some eighteen centuries before Copernicus, and why ancient astronomers rejected his idea, including the puzzle of the missing stellar parallax.

Explain how, in 2008, an attempt by Pakistan's telecom authority to block YouTube domestically accidentally knocked the site offline across much of the world, using the episode to reveal how the internet's routing system runs largely on trust.

Explain the leading theories about why the Nazca people etched giant hummingbirds, monkeys and arrow-straight lines into the Peruvian desert, and how they could have laid out figures that can only be seen whole from the air.

topic: Pillars of Creation in Eagle Nebula
prompt: Write an evocative description of the Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula, towers of cold gas and dust light-years tall in which new stars are being born.

Explain simulated annealing, the optimization technique borrowed from metallurgy, by showing how deliberately accepting occasional bad moves while slowly 'cooling' helps a search escape false peaks and settle into a near-optimal solution.

Explain the moving sofa problem, which asks for the largest shape that can be manoeuvred around a right-angled corner in a hallway, and why such a homely question kept mathematicians busy for decades.

Explain how mathematicians of the Kerala school in medieval India, beginning with Madhava of Sangamagrama, discovered infinite series for pi and trigonometric functions centuries before Newton and Leibniz.
Explain why the Tacoma Narrows Bridge twisted itself apart in a moderate wind in 1940, and why the popular account blaming simple resonance misses the real culprit, aeroelastic flutter.
Write a lyrical description of a fairy ring of mushrooms appearing overnight in a meadow, blending the folklore of elfin dances with the hidden fungus spreading outward underground year after year.
Describe the 'guest star' that Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054, bright enough to be seen in daylight for weeks, and the Crab Nebula with its spinning pulsar that it left behind.

Explain how the Inca built walls at Machu Picchu from stones fitted so tightly, without mortar, that a knife blade cannot slip between them, and why these walls have outlasted earthquakes that toppled later buildings.

Explain the solar neutrino problem, from a tank holding hundreds of thousands of litres of dry-cleaning fluid deep in a South Dakota gold mine that caught only a third of the expected neutrinos, to its resolution through neutrino oscillations.

topic: a walk through a dog's sense of smell
prompt: Describe a walk around the block from a dog's point of view, experienced almost entirely through smell, with every lamppost a layered newspaper of scents.

topic: tree rings as a climate archive
prompt: Explain how tree rings serve as a natural archive of past droughts, volcanic eruptions and even solar storms, allowing scientists to date events to the exact year.
Explain Michael Faraday's 1831 discovery that moving a magnet through a coil of wire creates an electric current, and how this simple observation now powers almost every generator on Earth.
Argue whether the Luddites, whose name has become shorthand for foolish resistance to progress, were in fact making a rational protest about who would benefit from the new textile machines.

topic: stopping the clocks after a death
prompt: Write a brief story set in a Victorian household where, following the old mourning custom, every clock in the house is stopped at the minute of a death, and a young child notices the strange silence where the ticking used to be.
Explain how the tallest trees, with no pump at all, pull water more than a hundred metres up from their roots to their highest leaves.

topic: Gregorian calendar and ten lost days
prompt: Explain why ten days simply vanished from the calendar in October 1582, describing how the Julian calendar slowly drifted against the seasons and how the Gregorian reform's clever leap-year rule brought Easter back into step with the spring equinox.

topic: Hyperbolic discounting, present versus future self
prompt: Write a second-person passage dramatizing hyperbolic discounting as a tug-of-war between your present self, who wants the dessert, the purchase and the lie-in, and your future self, who will have to pay for them.

Explain the 'ELIZA effect,' named after a simple 1960s chatbot that imitated a psychotherapist by turning users' statements back into questions, and why people, including its creator's own secretary, so readily credited it with understanding and empathy.

Describe what it would be like to be Stanislav Petrov on the night of 26 September 1983, sitting at a Soviet early-warning console as the screens insisted that American missiles were on their way and he had only minutes to decide whether to believe them.

topic: Sum of naturals equals minus one-twelfth
prompt: Explain the notorious claim that 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ... equals −1/12, clarifying in what sense this is nonsense, in what sense it is meaningful, and why the value nonetheless surfaces in theoretical physics.

topic: perceptron, XOR and first AI winter
prompt: Explain why Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron, hailed in 1958 as the embryo of a thinking machine, could not learn something as simple as the exclusive-or function, and how a famous critique of this limitation helped plunge neural network research into its first winter.

Write a lyrical description of the vast web of strangers, from loggers and graphite miners to chemists and shippers, whose uncoordinated cooperation produces a single ordinary wooden pencil, though no one person on Earth knows how to make one alone.

topic: the brain as a prediction machine
prompt: Explain the theory that the brain is fundamentally a prediction machine that constantly guesses what the senses will report and mainly perceives its own errors, in a style that would intrigue a general reader.
Explain how the human liver can regrow to its full size after much of it is removed, nodding to the myth of Prometheus, whose liver was devoured each day and restored each night.
Write a vivid account of the 1938 moment when a museum curator in South Africa spotted a strange blue fish among a trawler's catch and recognized a coelacanth, thought extinct for 66 million years.

topic: Aphantasia and the blind mind's eye
prompt: Write a quiet reflective passage from the point of view of someone with aphantasia who only discovered in adulthood that when other people 'picture a sunset', they actually see one in their minds.
Explain why animals play, from ravens sliding down snowy roofs to young rats wrestling, and what purpose such seemingly useless activity might serve.
Write a short story about Martha, the last passenger pigeon, living out her final days at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1914, a century after flocks of billions darkened American skies.
Describe the wildebeest migration's crossing of the Mara River, capturing the hesitation on the bank, the plunge and the crocodiles waiting below.
Describe the bustling community living inside a single rotting log on a forest floor, as if narrated by a naturalist peering through a magnifying glass.

Write a reflective passage explaining the Japanese art of kintsugi, in which broken pottery is mended with lacquer dusted in gold, and what it suggests about treating damage as part of an object's history rather than something to hide.
Explain 'Dutch disease', how the discovery of a huge natural gas field in the Netherlands ended up hurting the country's manufacturing exports, and why sudden resource windfalls can become a curse.

topic: Heron's aeolipile and a lost industrial revolution
prompt: Argue whether the ancient Greco-Roman world, which already possessed Heron of Alexandria's spinning steam-powered aeolipile, could have sparked an industrial revolution, and what ultimately held it back.

topic: hearing through a new cochlear implant
prompt: Describe the moment a person who has been deaf for years hears sound for the first time as their cochlear implant is switched on.

Explain Moravec's paradox, the observation that feats humans find hard, like chess and calculus, are easy for computers while things we do without thinking, like folding laundry or recognizing a friend in a crowd, are fiendishly difficult, and why evolution might explain the reversal.

topic: Zhuangzi's parable of the useless tree
prompt: Write a short, gentle piece explaining Zhuangzi's parable of the gnarled, useless tree that no carpenter would cut down and so lived to a great age, and what it suggests about the hidden value of uselessness.

Argue whether a dark, star-filled night sky should be protected as part of our natural heritage, the way we protect ancient forests and wild coastlines, given that most city dwellers can no longer see the Milky Way.

topic: Kintsugi and the beauty of repair
prompt: Write a reflective passage about the Japanese practice of kintsugi, mending broken pottery with lacquer and gold, as a philosophy that treats breakage and repair as part of an object's history rather than something to hide.
Describe how a candle flame behaves aboard a space station, where, with no hot air rising, it burns as a dim, blue, nearly spherical glow.

Write a lyrical description of the undersea fiber-optic cables lying on the dark ocean floor, beginning with the words 'Beneath the waves,' as they carry pulses of light holding video calls, love letters and stock trades between continents.
Write an evocative description of the sangaku of Edo-period Japan, painted wooden tablets of geometry problems hung in Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples as offerings to the gods.

topic: Molyneux's problem of newly gained sight
prompt: Write a vivid passage explaining Molyneux's problem: if a person born blind who knew a cube and a sphere by touch suddenly gained sight, could they tell which was which just by looking, and what have studies of patients gaining sight after cataract surgery suggested?
Write an evocative passage imagining Sisyphus at the summit of his mountain as the boulder rolls back down, during the walk of descent when, as Camus insists, we must imagine him happy.

Explain the 1986 'congestion collapse' that slowed early internet links to a crawl, and how TCP congestion control, backing off sharply when packets are lost and creeping back up slowly, taught millions of computers to share the road politely.
Explain the concept of a star's habitable zone, or 'Goldilocks zone,' and why being inside it is neither necessary nor sufficient for a world to have liquid water.

topic: tea leaf paradox and meandering rivers
prompt: Explain the tea leaf paradox, why stirred tea leaves gather at the center of the cup instead of flinging outward, and how Einstein used the same idea to explain why rivers meander.
Explain memory reconsolidation, the discovery that recalling a memory makes it briefly unstable and open to revision, and why this means remembering is closer to re-creating than to replaying.
Write a haunting, lyrical description of false vacuum decay, imagining a bubble of 'true vacuum' expanding at nearly the speed of light and silently rewriting the laws of physics as it goes.

topic: Accounting tokens and the birth of writing
prompt: Explain the theory that writing was invented in ancient Mesopotamia not by poets or priests but by bookkeepers, tracing how small clay tokens standing for sheep and grain, sealed inside clay envelopes, gradually evolved into cuneiform.
Explain how soap films behave like tiny analog computers that solve Plateau's problem, instantly finding the surface of least area that spans any bent wire frame you dip into the solution.

Argue whether data compression and intelligence are fundamentally the same thing, as the founders of the Hutter Prize contend, considering what it really means to predict the next symbol in a text well.
Explain Euclid's two-thousand-year-old proof that the prime numbers never run out, showing how multiplying all the known primes together and adding one leads to an inescapable contradiction.
Compare Heraclitus' view that everything is in flux, like an ever-living fire, with Parmenides' claim that change is an illusion and that true being is one and unchanging.

Explain the coronal heating problem, why the Sun's thin outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its visible surface, which is rather like the air growing hotter as you walk away from a campfire.

topic: Change blindness in the door study
prompt: Narrate, from the perspective of a pedestrian giving directions, the 'door study' in which the stranger asking the way is swapped for a different person while a large door is carried between them, and the pedestrian never notices.
Explain Wittgenstein's remark that if a lion could speak, we could not understand him, and what it suggests about how language is woven into a shared form of life.
Explain why the famous 14-15 sliding puzzle craze of the 1880s, which challenged players to swap just two tiles, was mathematically impossible to solve, using the idea of the parity of a permutation.
Describe the legendary experiment in which Blaise Pascal burst a sturdy wooden barrel by pouring a small amount of water into a tall, thin tube inserted into its lid.
Write a playful, lyrical description of pareidolia, the mind's irresistible habit of finding faces in electrical outlets, burnt toast, drifting clouds and the front grilles of cars.
Explain how a Venus flytrap counts, snapping shut only after two touches of its trigger hairs within about twenty seconds and beginning digestion only after further touches.

topic: Magellan's crew and the lost day
prompt: Write a brief story in which the exhausted survivors of Magellan's circumnavigation reach the Cape Verde islands in 1522 and discover, to their bewilderment, that their carefully kept logbook is one full day behind the calendar on shore.

topic: rocky tide pool at low tide
prompt: Write a vivid description of a rocky tide pool at low tide, as anemones, crabs and sea stars endure the hours between the sea's departure and its return.

topic: the last payphone on the corner
prompt: Write a melancholy, slightly humorous reflection from the point of view of the last working payphone on a city street corner, remembering the urgent calls, whispered confessions and pocketfuls of coins it once received.
Write a brief story about the young Mary Anning on the stormy cliffs of Lyme Regis in the early 1800s, uncovering the skeleton of an ichthyosaur.

Explain Pólya's recurrence theorem, which says a drunkard stumbling randomly around an endless city grid will surely find their way home, whereas a drunk bird flitting randomly through three-dimensional space may be lost forever.

Explain adversarial examples in image recognition, where adding a carefully crafted pattern of noise invisible to humans can make a neural network confidently mistake a panda for a gibbon, and what this reveals about how differently machines 'see.'
Explain how the parasitic vine dodder, lacking roots and leaves of its own, 'sniffs' the air for chemical cues to choose and coil around its host plants.

topic: inside a quantum computer's dilution refrigerator
prompt: Describe what it would be like to shrink down and stand inside the gleaming, chandelier-like dilution refrigerator of a quantum computer, colder than outer space, where fragile qubits must be shielded from even the faintest whisper of heat.
Describe what it would be like to live with locked-in syndrome, fully aware and thinking but able to communicate only by blinking one eye.

Explain how Henrietta Swan Leavitt, cataloguing stars on photographic plates at Harvard, discovered the link between a Cepheid variable's brightness and its pulsing period, handing astronomers a yardstick for measuring the universe.

Write a brief story in which Alexander the Great, master of half the known world, visits the philosopher Diogenes lounging in the sun at Corinth and offers him any wish, only to be asked to step out of his light.

Explain the weak anthropic principle through Douglas Adams' image of a puddle that marvels at how perfectly its hole fits it, and what this means for arguments that the universe is fine-tuned for life.
Explain how a whisper spoken against the wall of the whispering gallery in St Paul's Cathedral can be heard clearly on the far side of the dome.

topic: Conjunction fallacy and the Linda problem
prompt: Explain the conjunction fallacy using the famous 'Linda problem', in which most people judge that a socially conscious philosophy graduate is more likely to be a feminist bank teller than simply a bank teller.
Explain how a microwave oven heats food by making water molecules jostle, and why it so often leaves frozen pockets in the middle of a dish.
Explain the anchoring effect, using the experiment in which spinning a rigged wheel of fortune swayed people's guesses about the percentage of African nations in the United Nations.
Describe the day the Chicxulub asteroid struck, from the blinding flash over the shallow sea of the Yucatán to the global firestorm and the long darkness that followed.
Describe the night of a mass coral spawning on the Great Barrier Reef, when, cued by moonlight and water temperature, countless corals release bundles of eggs and sperm at once.

Explain why there is no general formula built from arithmetic and roots that solves every fifth-degree polynomial equation, as Ruffini and Abel showed, and how thinking about the symmetries among an equation's roots reveals the deeper reason.
Narrate the sixteenth-century feud between Niccolò Tartaglia and Gerolamo Cardano over the secret formula for solving cubic equations, a tale of public mathematical duels, sworn oaths, and betrayal.
Explain the Soviet fox domestication experiment, in which breeding silver foxes only for tameness produced, within a few decades, floppy ears, curly tails and piebald coats.

topic: Cavendish banana clones and Panama disease
prompt: Explain why nearly all the bananas sold in supermarkets are genetically identical clones, and how this leaves the Cavendish banana vulnerable to a fungal disease that already wiped out its predecessor.
Explain quorum sensing, the way bacteria release and detect chemical signals to count their own numbers and act together only once a crowd has gathered.

Write a brief story in which an elderly Mark Twain, who was born the year Halley's Comet appeared and joked that he expected to go out with it, watches the night sky in the spring of 1910 as the comet returns.

topic: The statue and the lump of clay
prompt: Explain the puzzle of the statue and the lump of clay: if a sculptor shapes clay into a statue, are there two objects in the same place at once, given that squashing it would destroy the statue but not the clay?

Describe how Craig Reynolds's 1986 'boids' simulation produced lifelike flocks on a computer screen from three simple rules, avoid crowding, align with neighbors and stay close, evoking a murmuration of starlings rising out of code.

topic: divergent fates of Venus, Earth, Mars
prompt: Compare how Venus, Earth and Mars, which began as broadly similar rocky planets, ended up as a scorching greenhouse, a living world and a frozen desert.

Explain how Zhang Heng's bronze seismoscope of 132 CE, ringed with eight dragons holding balls above eight open-mouthed toads, could announce a distant earthquake and hint at the direction it came from.

Write a haunting passage explaining blindsight, the eerie condition in which people blinded by damage to the visual cortex can still point to objects and step around obstacles they insist they cannot see.
Describe what it would be like to live with prosopagnosia, recognizing friends and family not by their faces but by their gait, voices, haircuts and the clothes they habitually wear.
Write an evocative passage about the small bands of modern humans who left Africa tens of thousands of years ago and whose descendants would eventually reach every continent but one.

topic: Sartre's bad faith and the waiter
prompt: Explain Sartre's concept of bad faith through his example of a cafe waiter whose movements are a little too precise, as if he were playing at being a waiter rather than freely choosing himself.
Write a lyrical retelling of Rousseau's stag hunt, in which hunters must decide whether to trust one another enough to pursue a stag together or each slip away to catch a sure but meager hare.
Explain, addressing the reader directly as 'you,' why your own voice sounds unfamiliar and often disappointing when you hear it played back on a recording.
Explain apoptosis, or programmed cell death, showing how the separation of fingers in a developing embryo depends on cells obediently dying.

topic: default mode network and mind wandering
prompt: Write a reflective passage in the second person about the mind wandering during a long shower, weaving in the brain's default mode network that springs to life when we stop focusing on the outside world.
Explain how the immune system can make antibodies against molecules it has never encountered, by shuffling gene segments like a slot machine that can produce billions of combinations.

Explain how the builders of the passage tomb at Newgrange in Ireland, some five thousand years ago, engineered a narrow roof-box so that at dawn around the winter solstice a thin beam of sunlight creeps down the passage to light the innermost chamber.

Explain the three-body problem and why, unlike two orbiting bodies, three bodies tugging on each other generally have no neat solution, as Henri Poincaré discovered while competing for a prize offered by the King of Sweden.
Explain the ultimatum game and why people across many cultures routinely reject small but free offers of money, defying the predictions of purely self-interested economic theory.

Explain why, in 1769, astronomers including James Cook's expedition to Tahiti travelled to the far corners of the globe to time Venus crossing the face of the Sun, and how this was meant to measure the size of the solar system.

topic: Kierkegaard's Abraham and the leap of faith
prompt: Explain Kierkegaard's reading of Abraham's journey to Mount Moriah in Fear and Trembling, and why he believed faith requires a leap beyond anything ethics or reason can justify.
Argue whether humans are still evolving by natural selection now that medicine and technology shield us from many of the pressures that shaped our ancestors.
Explain the winner's curse, opening with the jar-of-coins auction in which the highest bidder almost always overpays, and showing how the same trap affects oil-field leases and corporate takeovers.

topic: Jenner, cowpox and the first vaccine
prompt: Explain how Edward Jenner's interest in milkmaids who had caught cowpox led to the first vaccine, and how the word 'vaccine' itself comes from the Latin for cow.

Describe our place within Laniakea, the immense supercluster whose galaxies, the Milky Way among them, flow toward a gravitational basin called the Great Attractor, using the image of rivers draining into a sea.

Write a short reflective passage about Augustine's confession that he knows what time is until someone asks him, dwelling on how the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the present has no width at all.
Explain Kant's notorious claim that you must not lie even to a murderer at the door asking where your friend is hiding, and what this case reveals about the logic of the categorical imperative.

Explain the bouba/kiki effect, the finding that people across many languages match a rounded blob to 'bouba' and a spiky shape to 'kiki', and what it implies about whether the sounds of words are truly arbitrary.
Describe, moment by moment, what happens inside the body in the first seconds after a hiker spots a snake on the trail, as adrenaline triggers the fight-or-flight response.

Describe lying in a dark field on an August night watching the Perseid meteor shower, knowing that each streak of light is a speck of dust shed long ago by the comet Swift-Tuttle, burning up the moment it meets our air.

topic: a homing pigeon in the First World War
prompt: Write a brief story about a homing pigeon carrying a desperate message across the battlefield in the First World War, guided by senses its handlers never understood.

topic: island rule of dwarfism and gigantism
prompt: Explain the island rule, which makes elephants shrink and rodents grow to giant size when they become stranded on islands, using examples like the dwarf mammoths of Wrangel Island.

topic: garter snake and rough-skinned newt arms race
prompt: Explain the evolutionary arms race between the rough-skinned newt, which carries enough toxin to kill several people, and the garter snakes that have evolved resistance in order to eat it.

Explain how the Ariane 5 rocket destroyed itself less than a minute into its first flight in 1996 because software reused from its predecessor tried to squeeze a 64-bit number into a 16-bit space, and what the disaster teaches about assumptions hidden in old code.

Explain the theory that the legendary Hanging Gardens of Babylon may never have stood in Babylon at all, but in the Assyrian capital of Nineveh, watered by King Sennacherib's ingenious aqueducts and bronze water-raising screws.

Explain David Lewis's modal realism, the startling view that every possible world, including one where you became a lighthouse keeper, is just as real as ours, and why a careful philosopher would defend it.

Explain the Jordan curve theorem, the seemingly obvious claim that every closed loop drawn on a flat plane without crossing itself has an inside and an outside, and why proving it rigorously turned out to be surprisingly difficult.

Write a short reflective passage about the young Werner Heisenberg on the barren North Sea island of Helgoland in 1925, recovering from hay fever and staying up until dawn as the mathematics of quantum mechanics fell into place.
Write an evocative passage about the blue note, the bent, in-between pitch at the heart of the blues, describing how it slides between major and minor and the feelings it carries.

Write a short explanatory passage on the Towers of Hanoi puzzle and the legend of monks moving sixty-four golden disks, showing how recursion turns a seemingly impossible task into one simple rule repeated inside itself.
Explain why the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador, not Mount Everest, is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's center.

topic: tulip breaking virus and tulip mania
prompt: Explain how the prized striped 'broken' tulips that fueled Dutch tulip mania owed their flames of color to a virus.

topic: Dutch tulip mania at its peak
prompt: Write a vivid passage describing the height of Dutch tulip mania in the winter of 1636-37, when single bulbs of flame-streaked tulips changed hands in smoky taverns for the price of a fine house.
Explain Hegel's master-slave dialectic, the story of two self-conscious beings struggling for recognition, and the twist by which the bondsman, through his labor, ends up with the deeper freedom.

topic: walking a solar system scale model
prompt: Describe, as a guide leading a group of walkers, a scale model of the solar system in which the Sun is the size of a beach ball, conveying how unimaginably empty space really is.

topic: unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in physics
prompt: Take a position on Eugene Wigner's 'unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics': is it a deep mystery that abstract equations describe the physical world so well, or is the fit less surprising than it seems?
Explain Pascal's Wager as if it were a high-stakes bet at a gambling table, and point out the strongest objections it faces, such as the problem of many possible gods.

Explain why a frozen lake can sing with eerie, laser-like pings and whoops as its ice expands, flexes and cracks, describing the sound as a lone skater standing in the middle of the lake would hear it.
Explain the 'Brazil nut effect,' the tendency of the largest nuts in a shaken can of mixed nuts to rise to the top even though they are heavier.

topic: Black Death arriving in a medieval town
prompt: Describe a medieval town in 1348 as the Black Death arrives, and weave in what modern science has learned about the bacterium Yersinia pestis and the fleas that carried it.

Write a brief story set on an island where no one may ever speak of eye color, in which a visitor's single innocent remark sets off an inexorable chain of logical deductions that ends, many days later, with a sudden mass departure.

Describe, in the second person, what it would be like to experience time as a processor does, where a clock cycle is a heartbeat, fetching data from main memory feels like waiting for a letter by sea, and reading from a spinning hard disk is a journey of years.
Write a short reflective passage about Ludolph van Ceulen, who devoted much of his life to computing pi to thirty-five decimal places and had the digits engraved on his tombstone.

topic: Ego depletion and the replication crisis
prompt: Argue whether ego depletion, the idea that willpower is a muscle that tires with use, should still be taught now that large multi-lab replication efforts have failed to find the effect.
Describe a walk through a Carboniferous coal swamp three hundred million years ago, among towering club mosses whose fallen trunks piled up because few organisms could yet rot wood.
Explain why chili peppers evolved capsaicin to burn the mouths of mammals while leaving birds, their preferred seed dispersers, entirely unbothered.

topic: serotinous pine cones opened by fire
prompt: Explain how some pines keep their cones sealed with resin for years until the heat of a wildfire melts them open, making fire a midwife rather than an enemy.

Describe Hannibal's army crossing the Alps in 218 BCE as the first autumn snows fell, with war elephants struggling along icy ledges and soldiers splitting rockfalls by heating them with fire and dousing them with sour wine.
Argue whether the interstellar visitor ʻOumuamua, with its elongated shape and unexplained acceleration, ever gave scientists good reason to consider that it might be alien technology.

topic: data center at three in the morning
prompt: Write an atmospheric description of a vast data center at three in the morning: rows of blinking servers, the roar of cooling fans, cold aisles and hot aisles, and the invisible tide of human requests flowing through it all.
Explain how a sourdough starter is a miniature ecosystem of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria that compete, cooperate and settle into a stable community over time.
Explain why the sky is blue at noon yet red and orange at sunset, using the image of sunlight running an obstacle course through the atmosphere.
Explain what would happen to Earth if the Sun suddenly vanished, including why we would keep orbiting and basking in its light for about eight minutes before noticing anything.
Explain Filippo Brunelleschi's mirror experiment in front of the Florence Baptistery and how it helped launch the mathematical linear perspective that transformed Renaissance painting.

topic: twilight ring of tidally locked planet
prompt: Describe what it would be like to live in the twilight ring of a tidally locked planet, where the sun hangs forever at the same point near the horizon, with scorching day on one side and frozen night on the other.
Explain the Miller-Urey experiment of 1952, in which electric sparks passed through a flask of simple gases produced amino acids, and why it electrified the search for life's origins.
Explain the physics of skipping a stone across water, including the ideal angle of impact and why spin is the secret to many bounces.

Explain the concept of 'desire paths', the bare dirt trails worn across lawns and parks where people refuse to follow the paved route, and reflect on what they reveal about the quiet disagreement between planners and the people who actually walk.

topic: sperm whale dive to hunt giant squid
prompt: Describe a sperm whale's dive into the lightless deep to hunt giant squid, holding its breath for an hour as it navigates by clicks.
Explain the IKEA effect, the tendency to overvalue things we have built or assembled ourselves, from wobbly flat-pack shelves to cake mixes that ask you to add your own egg.

topic: stellar origins of the body's elements
prompt: Explain in lyrical prose how the calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were forged inside ancient stars and scattered by their violent deaths, so that every human body is assembled from stellar debris.
Describe the uncanny experience of highway hypnosis, when a driver arrives safely home after miles of familiar road with no memory of having made a single turn.

Explain the mystery of the Namib Desert's fairy circles, the millions of bare rings of earth dotting its grasslands, and the competing theories of sand termites versus self-organising grasses, in a tone of open-ended wonder.

topic: a cuckoo chick in a reed warbler nest
prompt: Write a brief story told from the perspective of a cuckoo chick hatching in a reed warbler's nest, pushing out the other eggs while its tiny foster parents work themselves ragged to feed it.
Describe what it would be like to be the only genuine participant in Solomon Asch's conformity experiment, watching one confederate after another confidently choose the obviously wrong line.
Describe what the sky would look like from one of the seven Earth-sized planets of the TRAPPIST-1 system, where neighbouring worlds can loom larger than the Moon in a dim, ruddy daylight.

Explain Derek Parfit's repugnant conclusion, showing step by step how plausible assumptions about adding happy lives seem to imply that an enormous population of lives barely worth living would be better than a smaller, flourishing one.

Explain the unexpected hanging paradox, in which a prisoner reasons step by step that a surprise execution next week is impossible and is then genuinely astonished when the hangman knocks on Wednesday.

topic: Doggerland lost beneath the North Sea
prompt: Write an elegiac, lyrical passage that begins with the words 'Beneath the trawlers' nets' about Doggerland, the lost lowland of forests, marshes and rivers that once joined Britain to mainland Europe before rising seas swallowed it some eight thousand years ago.

topic: the body in Everest's death zone
prompt: Describe what happens to the human body in the 'death zone' above eight thousand meters on Everest, where each breath carries only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level.

Describe what it would be like to be Hayy ibn Yaqzan, the child in Ibn Tufayl's medieval tale who grows up alone on an island, raised by a gazelle, and reasons his way from the stars to the nature of God.

Describe what it would be like to buy a loaf of bread in Berlin during the hyperinflation of 1923, when prices rose by the hour and workers were paid twice a day so they could spend their wages before they became worthless.
Explain what would actually happen to a human body exposed to the vacuum of space without a suit, correcting the movie myths of exploding heads and instant freezing.
Describe what it would be like to hear Silbo Gomero, the whistled language of La Gomera in the Canary Islands, as shepherds send whole sentences echoing across deep volcanic ravines.

topic: Young Gauss summing one to hundred
prompt: Write a short, charming narrative of the schoolroom legend in which the young Carl Friedrich Gauss stunned his teacher by adding up all the numbers from 1 to 100 in a matter of moments.
Write a reflective passage about the Christmas season of 1758, when the comet Edmond Halley had predicted returned on schedule, sixteen years after his death.

topic: Aristotle's doctrine of the golden mean
prompt: Explain Aristotle's doctrine of the golden mean, showing how courage sits between cowardice and recklessness, and why the right middle is not a mathematical average but depends on the person and the situation.

Describe the world as experienced by someone with akinetopsia, or motion blindness, for whom pouring a cup of tea becomes a series of frozen snapshots in which the liquid seems to leap from empty to overflowing.

Write a reflective passage imagining Pierre de Fermat jotting in the margin of his copy of Diophantus that he had a truly marvellous proof the margin was too narrow to contain, and the 358-year chase that note set in motion.

Explain how tidal friction is slowly lengthening Earth's day and pushing the Moon away, and how growth rings in fossil corals reveal that a year in the Devonian period lasted around four hundred days.
Explain why a fresh snowfall makes the world sound so hushed, describing how the porous lattice of newly fallen snow swallows sound waves, in a passage that opens on an empty city street at midnight.
Write a lyrical description of a newborn's first breath, when the lungs inflate, the blood reroutes and an opening between the heart's chambers begins to close within minutes of birth.

Write a dreamy, lyrical passage about Zhuangzi waking from a dream of being a butterfly and no longer knowing whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly or a butterfly now dreaming he is a man.
Explain why snowflakes grow with six-fold symmetry and why, as the photographer Wilson Bentley suggested after capturing thousands of them, no two seem to be alike.
Explain epiphenomenalism through Thomas Huxley's image of consciousness as the whistle of a steam locomotive, which accompanies the engine's work but contributes nothing to moving the train.
Explain the expansion of the universe using the analogy of raisins in a rising loaf of bread, making clear why every galaxy sees the others receding and why the expansion has no center.
Write a lyrical passage about the monarch butterfly migration, in which the butterflies that reach the Mexican mountain forests are the great-grandchildren of those that left them the year before.
Explain the mammalian diving reflex, which slows the heart and shifts blood toward the core when the face meets cold water, and how it has helped people survive long submersions.

topic: tears of wine and Marangoni effect
prompt: Describe the 'tears' or 'legs' that climb and fall on the inside of a glass of wine, and the Marangoni effect that drives them.

Explain the St. Petersburg paradox, a coin-tossing game with an infinite expected payout that nobody sensible would pay much to play, and how Daniel Bernoulli's idea of diminishing utility attempted to resolve it.
Write a brief story about Benjamin Franklin's kite experiment in a thunderstorm, told from the point of view of his son, who stands beside him in the field.
Argue that getting lost, wandering an unfamiliar city without GPS until the streets turn strange, is an experience worth preserving in an age when we always know exactly where we are.

Explain the Sleeping Beauty problem, in which a woman is woken once or twice depending on a coin toss and has her memory of each waking erased, and why philosophers still argue over whether her confidence in heads should be one half or one third.
Explain Karl Popper's idea of falsifiability by contrasting the 1919 eclipse test of Einstein's theory, which genuinely risked failure, with theories that can explain away any possible outcome.
Argue whether the Mpemba effect, the claim that hot water can freeze faster than cold water, is a genuine physical phenomenon or an artifact of poorly controlled experiments.

Narrate a classroom playing Martin Shubik's dollar auction, in which a single dollar bill is auctioned but the second-highest bidder must also pay, and show how perfectly rational bids escalate until people are paying several dollars for one.
In a warm, conversational tone, explain the fundamental attribution error using the example of a driver who cuts you off in traffic, and how differently you judge yourself when you do the same thing.

Explain Hume's puzzle of the missing shade of blue, in which a person who has seen every shade but one can nevertheless imagine the gap, and why this small case threatens his own theory that all ideas come from impressions.

Retell, in the cadence of an ancient legend, the story of the Lo Shu magic square that appeared on the shell of a turtle emerging from the flooded river Lo, and convey why its numbers were held sacred.

topic: Gettier problem and the stopped clock
prompt: Explain the Gettier problem using the example of someone who glances at a stopped clock that happens to show the correct time, and show why a justified true belief might still fall short of knowledge.
Explain the painter's paradox of Gabriel's horn, a trumpet-shaped solid that holds a finite amount of paint yet has a surface so infinite that no amount of paint could ever coat it.

Describe Otto von Guericke's seventeenth-century demonstration with the Magdeburg hemispheres, in which teams of horses strained and failed to pull apart two copper half-spheres held together by nothing but the pressure of the air.

Explain the Wigner's friend thought experiment for a general audience, in which one observer measures a quantum system inside a sealed lab while another waits outside, and why it raises the question of whether facts can differ between observers.
Explain Thomas Nagel's question 'What is it like to be a bat?' and why our inability to imagine echolocation from the inside poses a challenge for purely physical accounts of the mind.
Explain the competing hypotheses for why zebras have stripes, and why experiments with horses wearing striped coats point to confusing biting flies.

topic: lynx and snowshoe hare population cycles
prompt: Explain the roughly ten-year boom-and-bust cycles of Canadian lynx and snowshoe hares, revealed by the fur-trading records of the Hudson's Bay Company.
Explain the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' that haunted classical physics and how Max Planck, in what he later called an act of desperation, introduced the quantum in 1900 to resolve it.
Compare the life strategies of r-selected and K-selected species, such as a cod releasing millions of eggs and an elephant raising a single calf for years.

Explain why there is no single reliable 'now' across a network of computers and how Leslie Lamport's logical clocks order events by cause and effect rather than by wall-clock time, drawing a gentle parallel to Einstein's relativity.

Argue whether Pluto should be considered a planet, weighing the International Astronomical Union's 2006 definition against the view of scientists who classify worlds by their geology rather than their orbits.
Explain how airplane wings really generate lift, and why the popular textbook explanation that air over the top must 'catch up' with the air underneath is wrong.
Describe the moment Hume recounts at the close of the first book of his Treatise, when the gloom of his skeptical philosophy dissolves over dinner, conversation and a game of backgammon with friends.

Explain Hermann Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve and the spacing effect, describing how he memorized thousands of nonsense syllables himself to discover that memory fades along a predictable slope that well-timed reviews can flatten.

Write an evocative passage tracing the bullwhip effect, following how a small uptick in diaper sales at a few stores swells into wild swings in orders by the time it reaches the factory and its raw-material suppliers.

topic: muon imaging of the Great Pyramid
prompt: Explain how physicists used cosmic-ray muons raining down from the upper atmosphere to peer inside the Great Pyramid of Giza and discover a large hidden void in 2017.
Explain how mathematicians use invariants to tell knots apart, and why proving that a tangled loop of string can never be undone without cutting is far harder than it first appears.

Describe the experience of the Ganzfeld effect, in which a person gazing into a uniform, featureless field of light while listening to steady white noise gradually begins to hallucinate shapes, colors and scenes.
Write a playful, reflective passage inspired by Montaigne's question of whether, when he plays with his cat, she is not amusing herself with him more than he is with her.

Explain what Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments revealed about how ordinary people can be led to deliver what they believe are dangerous electric shocks, and which situational factors made defiance more likely.

topic: Socrates' final day and the hemlock
prompt: Write a vivid, evocative passage describing Socrates' last day in an Athenian prison in 399 BCE, from his refusal to escape to the calm with which he drinks the hemlock.

Write a vivid scene describing the audience at Douglas Engelbart's 1968 'Mother of All Demos' in San Francisco as they watched, for the first time, a computer mouse, clickable hypertext links and real-time collaborative editing on a screen.
Explain, using second person throughout, why no two people ever see exactly the same rainbow, since each arc is made of different raindrops sitting at a fixed angle to each viewer's own eye.
Explain Chien-Shiung Wu's 1956 experiment with cobalt-60 and why its revelation that nature can tell left from right shocked physicists who assumed the laws of physics were mirror-symmetric.
Explain Aristotle's four causes by walking through the making of a bronze statue, showing how material, form, maker and purpose each answer a different kind of 'why?'

Explain abductive reasoning, or inference to the best explanation, by examining how Sherlock Holmes concludes from a tan and a soldierly bearing that Dr. Watson has been in Afghanistan, and why this is not strictly deduction at all.

Explain what the Riemann hypothesis claims about the hidden rhythm of the prime numbers, and why so much of modern number theory hangs on whether the zeros of the zeta function all lie on a single critical line.

topic: Basic color terms and missing blue
prompt: Explain Berlin and Kay's research on basic color terms, which found that languages tend to acquire color words in a predictable order, and why so many ancient texts seem to lack a distinct word for blue.

Explain how quantum tunneling allows protons in the Sun's core to fuse even though, by classical physics, they lack the energy to overcome their mutual repulsion, so that without this quantum loophole the Sun would not shine.

Explain what a sourdough starter really is, a living community of wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria captured from flour and air, and why bakers speak of feeding it, naming it and passing it down through families like an heirloom.

Write a brief, humorous story about the 'Pauli effect,' the legend that the mere presence of the theorist Wolfgang Pauli caused laboratory equipment to fail, told from the viewpoint of a nervous lab technician.

Describe the maiden voyage of the magnificent Swedish warship Vasa in 1628, which sailed little more than a kilometre before a gust of wind heeled it over and sank it in Stockholm harbour in front of a stunned crowd.
Explain the Advaita Vedanta image of a rope mistaken for a snake in the dusk, and how it illustrates the idea that the world of separate things may be superimposed on a single underlying reality.
Explain how beavers act as ecosystem engineers, turning streams into wetlands that store water, resist wildfire and support a surge of other species.

Write a vivid description, in a quiet and wondering tone, of the natural nuclear reactors that switched themselves on and off in the uranium deposits of Oklo, Gabon, some two billion years ago, long before any human existed.

Explain the mere-exposure effect, the tendency to grow fond of faces, songs and even nonsense words simply because we have encountered them before, opening with the image of a song you disliked on first listen.
Explain Newcomb's paradox to a curious teenager, describing the near-infallible predictor, the two boxes, and why brilliant thinkers split sharply between taking one box and taking both.
Explain the square-cube law and why it means a giant scaled up from a human would collapse under its own weight, while a mouse can survive a fall down a deep mine shaft.

topic: a lost glove on a railing
prompt: Write a short reflective passage about a single lost glove that a stranger has carefully placed on top of a park railing so its owner might find it, considering the small, anonymous kindness of that gesture.
Explain the intricate partnership between figs and fig wasps, in which each fig species depends on its own tiny wasp to pollinate flowers hidden inside the fruit.

Explain the brachistochrone problem posed by Johann Bernoulli in 1696, showing why the fastest slide between two points is not a straight line but a cycloid, the curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel.
Write a vivid passage about the 1919 eclipse expeditions to the island of Príncipe and to Sobral in Brazil, where clouds, heat and anxious astronomers tested whether starlight bends around the Sun.
Describe the evening in late 1895 when Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a screen glowing across his darkened laboratory, and the haunting first X-ray image of his wife's hand, its bones and wedding ring.
Explain the faint young Sun paradox: why early Earth seems to have had liquid water even though the young Sun shone roughly thirty percent more dimly than it does today.

Explain how hummingbirds survive cold nights by slipping into torpor, letting their racing hearts and body temperature fall dramatically until dawn, describing the bird as a tiny flame turned down to an ember.

topic: why time speeds up with age
prompt: Write a reflective passage explaining why time seems to speed up as we grow older, drawing on the ideas that each year becomes a smaller fraction of our lives and that routine leaves fewer fresh memories to mark its passing.

Explain Arrow's impossibility theorem and why no ranked voting system can satisfy a handful of seemingly obvious fairness conditions all at once, using a simple example of three friends choosing a restaurant.

Explain how a Bloom filter can say with certainty that something is not in a set while only ever answering 'probably yes' otherwise, and why trading a little doubt for enormous memory savings is such a clever bargain.

Describe the final minutes of Apollo 11's descent to the Moon in July 1969, when the guidance computer flashed unfamiliar '1202' alarms and Neil Armstrong steered the Eagle past a field of boulders with fuel running out.
Argue whether conservation should practice triage, focusing resources on species most likely to be saved or most important to ecosystems rather than charismatic animals like the giant panda.

Explain Euler's polyhedron formula, vertices minus edges plus faces equals two, and why this humble count turns out to be a deep fingerprint of a shape's topology that distinguishes a sphere from a doughnut.
In a wry, slightly satirical tone, explain Veblen goods, the luxuries whose appeal grows as their price rises, and what Thorstein Veblen meant by conspicuous consumption.
Write a brief story unfolding over several January nights in 1610, as Galileo watches four small 'stars' shift position around Jupiter and realizes they are moons.

Describe what it would be like to sit alone in an anechoic chamber, one of the quietest rooms on Earth, where within minutes you begin to hear your own heartbeat, the rush of blood in your ears and the faint creak of your joints.
Explain why ice floats on water, unlike the solid forms of almost every other substance, imagining the perspective of a fish overwintering safely beneath a frozen lake.

topic: Code of Hammurabi's justice by rank
prompt: Explain what the Code of Hammurabi, carved on a black stone stele nearly four thousand years ago, reveals about Babylonian ideas of justice, including why its famous 'eye for an eye' depended on whether the victim was a noble, a commoner or a slave.
Argue whether mathematics is discovered or invented, taking a clear position and confronting the strongest objection to your view.

topic: why time seems to slow during danger
prompt: Explain why time seems to slow down during a car crash or a fall, and what experiments with volunteers dropped from great heights suggest about whether the brain truly speeds up or simply records memories more densely.
Explain how Ignaz Semmelweis discovered in 1840s Vienna that doctors coming straight from autopsies were spreading deadly childbed fever, and why his call for handwashing was ridiculed.
Argue whether gene drives should be used to wipe out the mosquito species that carry malaria, weighing millions of human lives against the unknown consequences of erasing a species.
Explain how Louis Pasteur's elegant swan-neck flasks, which let in air but trapped dust, finally defeated the age-old belief that life springs spontaneously from rotting broth.

Explain how the Renaissance book hunter Poggio Bracciolini's 1417 rediscovery of Lucretius' poem On the Nature of Things in a German monastery helped reintroduce the ancient idea of atoms and a universe without design to European thought.
Argue whether the Stanford prison experiment still deserves its place in psychology textbooks, considering later revelations that guards were coached and some participants were playing a role.

topic: Diary of Merer and pyramid logistics
prompt: Explain what the Diary of Merer, the oldest inscribed papyrus ever found, reveals about how an ordinary crew of boatmen ferried limestone blocks along the Nile and its canals to build the Great Pyramid of Giza.

Explain fast radio bursts, millisecond flashes of radio waves from distant galaxies that release as much energy as the Sun does in days, and how astronomers have begun to trace some of them to magnetars.

Explain how a laser works, focusing on stimulated emission and using the metaphor of a marching band whose members step in perfect unison to show why laser light differs from the light of an ordinary bulb.

topic: why reaching the Sun is hard
prompt: Explain why it takes far more rocket energy to send a probe into the Sun than to fling it out of the solar system entirely.
Describe the lunar dust that Apollo astronauts tracked back into their spacecraft: jagged, clinging, abrasive, and smelling, they reported, like spent gunpowder.
Write a short reflective passage on the idea that the calcium in our bones and the iron in our blood were forged inside stars that lived and died before the Sun was born.

Describe the bustling Mediterranean trading world in which young Leonardo of Pisa, later called Fibonacci, learned Hindu-Arabic numerals from North African merchants and brought them to Europe in his Liber Abaci of 1202.

Explain the long-term evolution experiment in which twelve populations of E. coli have been propagated daily since 1988, and why the sudden appearance of a strain able to feed on citrate was such a striking moment.

Explain the Boltzmann brain paradox in a tone of playful unease, describing the argument that in some cosmological models a lone, fleeting brain fluctuating out of chaos should be far more likely than an entire ordered universe like ours.

Write a dramatic narrative of the bitter priority dispute between Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz over who invented calculus, including the supposedly impartial Royal Society report that Newton secretly drafted himself.

Explain how the Haber-Bosch process, which pulls nitrogen out of thin air to make fertilizer, became arguably the most consequential invention of the twentieth century, to the point that roughly half the nitrogen in our bodies has passed through a factory.
Explain the Elitzur–Vaidman bomb tester, a thought experiment showing how quantum interference could, in principle, confirm that a bomb is live without a single photon ever touching it.

topic: Husserl's epoche and a coffee cup
prompt: Describe what it would be like to apply Husserl's phenomenological epoche to a cup of morning coffee, setting aside every assumption about the outside world and attending only to how the cup shows itself to experience.

topic: Aristophanes' myth of the split humans
prompt: Write a lyrical retelling of the myth Aristophanes tells in Plato's Symposium, in which the first humans were round, four-armed creatures split in two by Zeus, so that love is the longing to find our other half.
Argue whether controlled nuclear fusion is a realistic future energy source or a mirage that will forever remain 'thirty years away.'
Explain the paradoxical idea of negative absolute temperature, which physicists have created in the laboratory and which is, in a precise sense, hotter than any positive temperature.
Using Bayes' theorem, explain to an anxious patient why a positive result on a 99%-accurate test for a very rare disease may still mean they are probably healthy.

Describe what it would have been like to stand behind Howard Carter in November 1922 as he widened a hole in a sealed doorway, held up a candle, and saw the glint of gold in Tutankhamun's tomb for the first time in more than three thousand years.
Explain the theory that hiccups are an evolutionary leftover from the gill-breathing of our amphibian ancestors, delivered with a light, humorous touch.

Describe what it would be like to drift in a hot-air balloon at dawn, where because you travel with the wind the air around you feels perfectly still and the only sounds are dogs barking far below and the occasional roar of the burner.
Explain Thomas Kuhn's notion of a paradigm shift, using the move from an Earth-centered to a Sun-centered cosmos to show how scientists can come to see the same sky in a completely new way.
Explain the long-standing puzzle of the Crookes radiometer, the light mill whose vanes spin in sunlight, and why the obvious explanation, the pressure of light, would actually turn it the wrong way.

topic: frame dragging and Gravity Probe B
prompt: Explain frame dragging, the prediction that a spinning mass like Earth twists spacetime around itself, and how the Gravity Probe B satellite used near-perfect spheres of quartz to measure it.

Explain the phenomenon of blindsight, in which people with damage to the visual cortex insist they see nothing yet can accurately point to or step around objects in their blind field, and what it reveals about vision without awareness.
Explain how Henry Cavendish, using lead spheres and a delicate torsion balance in a shed, measured the faint gravitational attraction between objects and thereby 'weighed the Earth' in 1798.

Explain how a dandelion seed can stay aloft for miles by creating a stable bubble of swirling air above its bristly parachute, a form of flight scientists only recently discovered, as if explaining it to a child about to blow on a dandelion clock.

Explain the RNA world hypothesis, which proposes that early life relied on RNA molecules able both to store information and to catalyze reactions, solving the chicken-and-egg problem of DNA and proteins.

Argue whether public fears that the Large Hadron Collider might create a black hole capable of swallowing the Earth deserved a serious scientific response, and what the episode teaches about communicating risk.

topic: petrichor and geosmin, the smell of rain
prompt: Explain where the smell of rain comes from, including the compound geosmin made by soil bacteria and the human nose's astonishing sensitivity to it.

Explain why a large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would threaten the encryption that protects online banking, and what security experts mean by the unsettling strategy of 'harvest now, decrypt later.'

Explain the quantum property called spin, including the bizarre fact that an electron must be rotated 720 degrees rather than 360 to return to its original state, using the 'belt trick' as an illustration.
Explain how the mantis shrimp strikes with a club so fast that the water around it briefly boils, creating collapsing cavitation bubbles that deliver a second blow.
Explain Frédéric Bastiat's broken window fallacy, in which a shattered shop window seems to stimulate the economy, and the 'unseen' costs that this reasoning overlooks.

Explain the relativity of simultaneity using Einstein's thought experiment of lightning striking both ends of a moving train, showing why two observers can honestly disagree about whether two events happened at the same time.
Describe how the night sky over Earth might change as the Andromeda galaxy swells and merges with the Milky Way over the next few billion years, addressing whatever beings may be watching then.

Explain regression to the mean, starting from Francis Galton's observations about the heights of parents and their children, and show how it creates illusions like the supposed 'Sports Illustrated cover jinx.'
Explain why a computer that can simulate colliding galaxies insists that 0.1 plus 0.2 does not quite equal 0.3, using the analogy of trying to write one-third exactly as a decimal.

topic: why the stomach doesn't digest itself
prompt: Explain why the stomach, filled with acid strong enough to dissolve many metals, does not digest itself.
Explain the Dzhanibekov effect, also known as the tennis racket theorem, in which a spinning wing nut or T-shaped handle in zero gravity unexpectedly flips over at regular intervals.
Explain why the ocean is blue, correcting the common belief that it simply reflects the colour of the sky.
Explain to a curious teenager why binary search can find one name among a billion in about thirty guesses, starting from the childhood game of guessing a secret number between one and a hundred.
Explain Gresham's law, the principle that 'bad money drives out good', using the image of people hoarding full-weight silver coins while spending the clipped and debased ones.

Write a brief story in which a programmer spends the last hours of December 31, 1999, watching a hospital's systems tick toward midnight, unsure whether the two-digit years she has spent months patching will hold.

Write a short reflective passage, addressed to the reader in the second person, about Heidegger's idea that facing the certainty of one's own death can wake a person from the everyday drift of doing what 'one' does.
Describe, from the perspective of a two-dimensional creature, what it would be like when a sphere from the third dimension passes through your flat world, as in Edwin Abbott's Flatland.
Explain how mRNA vaccines work by giving cells a temporary recipe for a harmless viral protein, using the analogy of a recipe card that is read and then shredded.
Write a vivid description of a star-nosed mole hunting in dark, wet soil, its twenty-two fleshy tentacles touching the world faster than the eye can follow.
Describe, in the second person, closing your eyes aboard a spacecraft and seeing sudden streaks and sparks of light caused by cosmic rays passing through your eyes.

topic: the figure inside a snow globe
prompt: Write a whimsical yet melancholy description of life from the point of view of the tiny figure inside a snow globe, whose entire weather depends on someone picking up the world and shaking it.

topic: Frankl and the last human freedom
prompt: Write a quiet, respectful reflective passage about Viktor Frankl's insight that even when everything else is taken away, a person retains the freedom to choose their attitude toward their circumstances.

topic: Brownian motion as proof of atoms
prompt: Explain how Einstein's 1905 analysis of the jittery dance of tiny particles suspended in water, known as Brownian motion, provided convincing evidence that atoms and molecules really exist.
Describe the week in July 1994 when the fragments of comet Shoemaker–Levy 9 slammed into Jupiter one after another, leaving dark bruises on the planet larger than the Earth.
Explain, with gentle humour, the physics behind why toast sliding off a table tends to land butter-side down, and why the answer has to do with the height of tables and of human beings.

topic: summer fog over the Golden Gate
prompt: Write a lyrical description of San Francisco's summer fog pouring over the hills and spilling through the towers of the Golden Gate Bridge like a slow white river, swallowing the city one street at a time.

topic: iron lungs and the polio vaccine
prompt: Describe a hospital ward in the early 1950s filled with rows of iron lungs breathing for children paralyzed by polio, and the relief that followed the arrival of a vaccine.
Explain Bertrand Russell's puzzle about the sentence 'The present King of France is bald,' and how his theory of descriptions handles talk about things that do not exist.

Compare circuit switching, the dedicated-line model of the old telephone network, with packet switching, in which messages travel as independently routed fragments, explaining why Paul Baran's Cold War vision of a network able to survive a nuclear attack favored the latter.
Explain the Maunder Minimum, the roughly seventy-year stretch in the seventeenth century when sunspots almost vanished, and the debate over its link to the harsh winters of the Little Ice Age.

Explain how the peppered moth of industrial England darkened as soot blackened tree bark and lightened again after clean air laws, making it a textbook case of natural selection observed in real time.

topic: Aztec philosophy of the slippery earth
prompt: Write a reflective passage on the Aztec saying that the earth is slippery and smooth, and the Nahua philosophy of seeking a balanced, well-rooted life on ground where it is so easy to fall.
Explain how magnetotactic bacteria build chains of tiny magnetic crystals inside their cells, turning themselves into living compass needles.

Explain how ancient Persians managed to make and store ice through scorching desert summers using towering domed mud-brick yakhchāls, shading walls, underground pits and the cold of the clear night sky.

topic: Diogenes searching for an honest man
prompt: Write a brief story in which Diogenes the Cynic wanders the streets of Athens in broad daylight with a lit lantern, searching for an honest man, and an encounter with a passerby teaches something unexpected.
Explain how physics might accommodate extra spatial dimensions curled up too small to see, using the analogy of an ant walking on a garden hose that looks like a one-dimensional line from far away.

topic: zoos as arks for endangered species
prompt: Argue whether modern zoos are justified as arks for endangered species, or whether their conservation role is overstated.

topic: Curse of knowledge, tappers and listeners
prompt: Explain the curse of knowledge using the 'tappers and listeners' experiment, in which people drumming out well-known songs with their fingers wildly overestimated how many listeners would recognize the tune.

Argue whether the many-worlds interpretation, in which every quantum measurement splits reality into branches, is a more honest reading of quantum mechanics than the Copenhagen view that observation collapses the wavefunction.

Explain, in a tone of quiet wonder, how John Conway's surreal numbers build from almost nothing a single number system containing the integers, the real numbers, infinite numbers, and infinitesimals all at once.

topic: satellite megaconstellations and the night sky
prompt: Argue whether the night sky should be protected as a shared human heritage against the thousands of bright satellites now streaking across astronomers' images.
Argue whether mathematical objects like numbers are discovered, existing independently of us like distant mountains, or invented, like the rules of chess.

topic: Quake III fast inverse square root
prompt: Explain the legend of the 'fast inverse square root' trick from the Quake III game engine, conveying in plain words how a mysterious magic number and some bit-level sleight of hand let 1990s computers light 3D worlds at astonishing speed.

Explain how the Mechanical Turk, a turbaned chess-playing automaton unveiled in 1770 that reportedly faced both Napoleon and Benjamin Franklin, fooled audiences across Europe and America for decades, and what was really hidden inside its cabinet.

Explain the phenomenon of 'grokking' in neural networks, where a model that has merely memorized its training data for a long stretch suddenly, long after its progress seems to stall, snaps into genuine understanding of the underlying rule.
