In a playful tone, explain what makes the Möbius strip a surface with only one side and one edge, and describe the surprising things that happen when you cut one down the middle.

Narrate the two-thousand-year struggle to prove Euclid's parallel postulate, culminating in the young János Bolyai's letter to his father announcing that he had created a strange new universe out of nothing.

topic: Borges' map the size of the empire
prompt: Write a short, whimsical passage about Borges' empire whose cartographers drew a map exactly the size of the territory, and what its tattered remains in the desert teach us about the difference between models and reality.
Argue whether mathematicians are right to accept the axiom of choice, given that it is enormously useful yet implies the existence of strange objects that no one could ever construct or describe.
Explain sonoluminescence, the mysterious flashes of light emitted by collapsing bubbles in sound-driven water, and how the snapping claw of the pistol shrimp produces a similar flash.

Describe October 14, 1947, when a bright orange rocket plane became the first aircraft to fly faster than sound in level flight, as the needle crossed Mach 1 and a boom rolled across the California desert.

Explain the priority inversion bug that kept rebooting the Mars Pathfinder lander in 1997, in which a low-priority task holding a shared resource blocked a high-priority one, and how engineers diagnosed and fixed it from millions of kilometers away.

Explain the 'walking moai' hypothesis for how the people of Rapa Nui moved multi-ton stone statues across their island by rocking them upright with ropes, and why the idea echoes local legends that the statues walked to their platforms.

topic: Nutmeg island of Run and Manhattan
prompt: Explain how the tiny nutmeg island of Run in the Banda Sea was once so precious that, under the 1667 Treaty of Breda, the Dutch were content to keep it and let the English hold on to a small colony called Manhattan instead.
Explain the paradox of Prince Rupert's drops, tadpole-shaped beads of glass whose heads can survive a hammer blow but which explode into powder if their thin tails are snapped.

Explain the reminiscence bump, the tendency of older adults to recall a disproportionate number of vivid memories from adolescence and early adulthood, and the competing theories for why those years loom so large.
Describe descending the thousands of geometric steps of the Chand Baori stepwell in Rajasthan toward the cool, dark water at its bottom on a blazing summer afternoon.

topic: Knowing the date of one's death
prompt: Argue whether you would want to know the exact date of your own death, and whether such knowledge would enrich or impoverish the life that remains.
Describe the life of an ancient bristlecone pine in the White Mountains of California, nearly five thousand years old and twisted by wind into living sculpture.

topic: rubber hand illusion and body ownership
prompt: Explain the rubber hand illusion, in which synchronized stroking makes a person feel that a fake hand on the table is their own, and what it reveals about how the brain builds a sense of body ownership.
Describe the song of a superb lyrebird in an Australian forest, which weaves together the calls of other birds and sometimes the sounds of camera shutters and chainsaws.

Describe, in second person, what it would be like to be a gnat caught in a drop of tree resin forty million years ago and slowly turned to amber, holding perfectly still while forests, ice ages and oceans come and go around you.
Describe the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883, whose explosion was heard nearly 5,000 kilometres away and whose pressure wave circled the globe several times, registering on barometers around the world.

topic: Toxoplasma making rats fearless of cats
prompt: Explain how the parasite Toxoplasma gondii appears to make infected rats lose their fear of cat urine, steering them toward the cats in whose guts it reproduces.

Write a reflective passage about a park bench bearing a small brass plaque in memory of someone who 'loved this view', imagining the many strangers who sit there each day without ever knowing who that person was.
Describe swimming through a giant kelp forest off the coast of California, with sunlight filtering through fronds that can grow half a meter in a single day.
Write a brief story in which Alexander Fleming returns from a summer holiday in 1928 to find a mold contaminating one of his bacterial plates, and notices the clear ring around it.
Explain Heisenberg's uncertainty principle to a curious teenager, making clear that it is a fundamental property of nature rather than a limitation of our measuring instruments.

Write a lyrical passage explaining the Japanese word komorebi, sunlight filtering through leaves, and the surprising fact that each soft dapple of light on the ground is really a tiny pinhole image of the sun itself.

topic: Four color theorem computer proof legitimacy
prompt: Argue whether the 1976 computer-assisted proof of the four color theorem, which checked far too many cases for any human to verify by hand, deserves to be called a genuine mathematical proof.
Explain how the observable universe can be about 93 billion light-years across even though it is only 13.8 billion years old.

Explain the monarch butterfly's migration between Canada and the mountain forests of central Mexico, a round trip that no single butterfly ever completes, and reflect on how a route can be 'remembered' by generations who have never flown it.

topic: Ubuntu: a person through other persons
prompt: Explain the southern African philosophy of Ubuntu, often summarized as 'a person is a person through other persons,' and how it offers a different picture of selfhood from the solitary individual of much Western thought.
Explain the liar paradox, 'This sentence is false,' in plain everyday language, and why such a tiny sentence has troubled logicians from ancient Greece to the twentieth century.

topic: Moore's paradox of belief and assertion
prompt: Explain Moore's paradox, the oddity of saying 'It is raining, but I don't believe it is raining,' a sentence that could easily be true yet seems absurd to assert.

Using the image of a spiral staircase that never quite returns to the floor it started on, explain the Pythagorean comma, why twelve perfect fifths overshoot seven octaves, and how equal temperament solved the problem by putting every interval very slightly out of tune.
Write a lyrical description of Emerson's moment crossing a bare common at twilight, when he felt himself become a 'transparent eyeball,' nothing in himself and wholly part of the currents of nature.

topic: packet trapped in a routing loop
prompt: Write a brief story told from the perspective of a single data packet trapped in a routing loop, bouncing between the same routers as the time-to-live counter stamped on its header ticks steadily down toward zero.
Describe what it might be like to stand before a traversable wormhole and gaze into its spherical mouth, seeing a warped image of the sky from a distant part of the universe.

topic: Le Guin's Omelas and its hidden child
prompt: Write an evocative passage describing the shimmering summer festival of Omelas from Ursula K. Le Guin's story, and the single suffering child in a basement upon whom all its happiness depends.

topic: Plato's myth of Theuth and writing
prompt: Explain the myth of Theuth and King Thamus in Plato's Phaedrus, in which the gift of writing is criticized for creating the appearance of wisdom while weakening memory, and why the worry feels newly relevant in the age of search engines.
Argue whether, if a safe technology could erase a painful memory forever, it would be wise to use it, considering what such memories contribute to who we are.

Explain Max Black's thought experiment of a universe containing nothing but two perfectly identical iron spheres, and how it challenges Leibniz's principle that no two distinct things can share all their properties.

Explain how James Clerk Maxwell, unifying electricity and magnetism in his equations, calculated the speed of electromagnetic waves and found it matched the speed of light, revealing what light actually is.

topic: Life in a taxicab geometry city
prompt: Describe, in the second person, what it would be like to live in a city governed by taxicab geometry, where distance can only be measured along the grid of streets and every 'circle' turns out to be a square.

Write a short narrative passage about the evening of October 29, 1969, when a student at UCLA tried to send the word 'LOGIN' to a computer at Stanford over the ARPANET and the system crashed after two letters, making the network's first message an accidental 'LO.'
Write a brief story in which a novice monk in a remote temple, moving golden disks in the legendary Tower of Brahma puzzle, works out how many ages remain before the world is said to end.
Explain, with gentle humor and a slice of Swiss cheese as a guide, the metaphysical puzzle of holes, which seem to be countable and measurable things and yet are made of nothing at all.
Explain the Penrose process, by which a sufficiently advanced civilization could in theory extract energy from a spinning black hole by sending objects into its ergosphere.

topic: Carl Woese and the discovery of archaea
prompt: Explain how Carl Woese, by comparing ribosomal RNA, discovered the archaea and redrew the tree of life into three great domains.

topic: Walter Benjamin's aura of the artwork
prompt: Explain Walter Benjamin's concept of the 'aura' of an original artwork and why he believed mechanical reproduction, from photography to film, was causing it to wither.
Argue whether conservationists should rewild landscapes by introducing elephants or other large animals as stand-ins for extinct Ice Age megafauna.
Explain how traditional Persian windcatchers and underground qanat channels worked together to cool desert homes without electricity, as if guiding a visitor through an old house in Yazd.
Write a reflective passage about turbulence, the swirling chaos in rising smoke and rushing rivers that remains one of the great unsolved problems of classical physics.

Explain the ancient link between perfect numbers and Mersenne primes, begun by Euclid and completed by Euler, and why volunteers around the world still donate their computers' idle time to hunting for ever larger examples.

topic: Meno's paradox and learning as recollection
prompt: Write a short passage explaining Meno's paradox, which asks how we can search for something we do not already know, and how Plato's Socrates answers it by coaxing an untutored slave boy to discover a geometric truth.

Explain how archaeologists traced Stonehenge's smaller bluestones to specific rocky outcrops in the Preseli Hills of Wales, more than 200 kilometres away, and the competing ideas about how Neolithic people managed to move them.
Explain why the real asteroid belt looks nothing like the crowded, rock-dodging fields of science fiction, and why spacecraft pass through it without any real danger of collision.
Write a lyrical description of listening to a Shepard tone, the auditory illusion of a pitch that seems to climb forever without ever actually getting higher.

Explain, with a touch of humor, why the wheel, often imagined as humanity's first great invention, appeared surprisingly late, only around 3500 BCE, and why the truly hard part was not the wheel but the axle.

topic: helium discovered in the Sun first
prompt: Explain how helium was discovered in the Sun's spectrum during a solar eclipse in 1868, nearly three decades before it was found on Earth, and how spectroscopy lets us read the chemistry of distant stars.
Explain garden-path sentences such as 'The old man the boat', and what the momentary confusion they cause reveals about how the brain builds meaning one word at a time.

Write a passage explaining the Gale-Shapley stable matching algorithm and how this piece of game theory became the basis for real systems that match medical residents to hospitals and kidney donors to patients.

topic: Frege's morning star and evening star
prompt: Explain Frege's distinction between sense and reference through the ancient discovery that the morning star and the evening star are the same planet, Venus, and why that identity was nevertheless real news.
Argue whether Marco Polo really travelled to China, weighing the vivid, accurate details of his account against its puzzling silences about the Great Wall, tea drinking and Chinese writing.

Explain, in an affectionate tone, what the dust drifting through a sunbeam in your living room is actually made of, from skin flakes, pollen and textile fibres to the occasional micrometeorite that has fallen from space onto your roof.

Explain Kant's puzzle of incongruent counterparts by inviting the reader to try fitting a left glove onto a right hand, and what the fact that mirror-image objects can never be made to coincide suggests about the nature of space.

topic: James Webb telescope unfolding in space
prompt: Describe the tense weeks after launch in December 2021 when the James Webb Space Telescope unfolded its tennis-court-sized sunshield and golden mirror segments on the way to its distant post.

Explain the curious physics of an hourglass, where sand trickles at a steady rate no matter how much remains above because the grains form arches that carry their own weight, and let the explanation drift into a meditation on how we measure time.
Explain why, when a Slinky hanging stretched from your hand is released, its bottom end seems to hover in mid-air until the collapsing top comes down to meet it.
Explain how a hurricane works as a giant heat engine, drawing energy from warm ocean water and releasing it high in the atmosphere, and why it weakens so quickly once it moves over land.

Explain the enduring mystery of Damascus steel, whose swirling watery patterns and legendary toughness came from a crucible technique lost by the eighteenth century, and what modern metallurgists found when they examined old blades under the microscope.
Describe the mammoth steppe of the last Ice Age, a vast cold grassland stretching from Europe to the Yukon that teemed with mammoths, woolly rhinos and cave lions.

Describe, in the second person, the trillions of neutrinos from the Sun streaming through your body every second, even at night, when they arrive having passed straight through the Earth beneath your bed.

topic: Coriolis effect and the toilet myth
prompt: Explain the Coriolis effect and why it shapes the spin of hurricanes but not the direction your sink or toilet drains, despite the popular myth.

Explain, in a playful tone, the 'gravity train' thought experiment, in which a straight tunnel bored through the Earth lets you fall from one end to the other in about forty-two minutes no matter where the tunnel goes.

Explain, with gentle humor, why language models that can compose sonnets have stumbled when asked to count the letter 'r' in 'strawberry,' tracing the problem to how text is chopped into tokens before the model ever sees it.

Write a reflective passage about the long life of Euclid's Elements, copied by scribes, carried through Arabic and Latin translations, and printed in more editions than almost any other book in history.

Write a lyrical description of wandering through Borges' Library of Babel, an endless honeycomb of hexagonal rooms containing every possible book, nearly all of them gibberish, where somewhere a true account of your own life must exist.
Explain how Tibetans adapted to life at high altitude partly through a gene variant likely inherited from Denisovans, an extinct group of archaic humans.
Explain how whales evolved from small, deer-like land mammals over roughly ten million years, tracing the fossil steps from walking ancestors to fully aquatic giants.
Explain Goodhart's law, the idea that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure, through examples such as factories meeting quotas by producing useless goods.
Write a lyrical description of Jupiter's Great Red Spot, a storm wider than Earth that has been churning for well over a century and a half and is slowly shrinking.

Write a short story in which Eratosthenes, librarian of Alexandria, hears of a well at Syene where the noon sun shines straight down on the solstice, and uses a shadow to measure the circumference of the whole Earth.

topic: Agloe, the trap town that became real
prompt: Write a brief story about Agloe, New York, a fictitious town inserted onto a 1930s road map as a copyright trap, told from the point of view of the person who later opened a real general store on that spot because the map said a town was there.

topic: why the blue LED was so hard
prompt: Explain why creating an efficient blue light-emitting diode was one of the great materials challenges of the twentieth century, and why its arrival finally made white LED lighting possible.
Explain how leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry but use them to cultivate a fungus garden, practicing a form of agriculture that began millions of years before humans.

Describe Adam Smith's pin factory as if you were walking through it, showing how dividing pin-making into about eighteen distinct operations allowed ten workers to produce tens of thousands of pins a day.
Explain why a candle flame is shaped like a teardrop on Earth but burns as a dim blue sphere aboard a space station, letting the flame itself seem a little bewildered by the sudden absence of 'up'.

topic: Paradox of fiction and real tears
prompt: Starting with the moment a reader weeps at the death of a beloved character, explain the paradox of fiction: how can genuine emotions be directed at someone we firmly believe never existed?

topic: Barnum effect and the fortune teller
prompt: Write a brief story in which a fairground fortune teller gives the same vague, flattering reading to three very different visitors, each of whom leaves convinced it described them perfectly.
Explain the story of Clever Hans, the horse who seemed to do arithmetic in early twentieth-century Berlin, and the lesson it left for everyone who studies animal minds.
Explain Simpson's paradox, in which a trend that holds within every subgroup reverses when the groups are pooled, using the famous 1973 Berkeley graduate admissions data as your central example.

topic: should aging be called a disease
prompt: Argue whether aging should be classified as a disease to be treated rather than accepted as an inevitable part of life.
Explain how most people alive today carry a small percentage of Neanderthal DNA, and what these inherited fragments may influence, from immune responses to skin and hair.
Explain why a spilled drop of coffee dries into a dark ring rather than a uniform stain, and why this everyday puzzle matters to people designing inkjet printers.

Describe the experience of looking at the famous duck-rabbit drawing as it flips from one animal to the other, and explore Wittgenstein's puzzle about what has changed when nothing on the page has changed.

Explain why old books smell the way they do, describing how the lignin and cellulose in aging paper break down into compounds with hints of vanilla and almond, in prose that makes a dusty secondhand bookshop feel alive.
Write a warm explanation of Aristotle's three kinds of friendship, those of utility, of pleasure and of virtue, and why he thought only the last kind is lasting and complete.

topic: glymphatic system cleaning the sleeping brain
prompt: Explain how the brain's glymphatic system flushes away metabolic waste during deep sleep, using the image of a city whose streets can only be hosed clean after the traffic stops.

Write a brief, comic story told from the point of view of Ea-nasir, the Mesopotamian copper merchant who received history's oldest known customer complaint, as he reads Nanni's furious clay tablet about substandard ingots.
Explain the phenomenon of 'booming' or singing sand dunes, whose avalanching grains can produce a deep hum heard for miles, beginning with the sentence 'The desert was not supposed to have a voice.'
Explain the physics behind the Challenger disaster of 1986, and how Richard Feynman demonstrated it at a televised hearing by dipping a piece of O-ring rubber into a glass of ice water.

Explain why every snowflake has six-fold symmetry and yet no two seem exactly alike, following a single ice crystal's tumbling fall through changing temperature and humidity as if it were writing its own autobiography.

Describe what it would be like to spend a summer week above the Arctic Circle under the midnight sun, when the sun circles the sky without ever setting and the line between one day and the next quietly dissolves.

Describe what it would be like to live in a universe shaped like a three-dimensional torus, where travelling far enough in any direction brings you back to your starting point and you might glimpse the back of your own head among the distant stars.

Describe what it would be like to swim in a cenote on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, a flooded limestone sinkhole the ancient Maya regarded as a gateway to the underworld, as columns of sunlight fall through the clear water from an opening far above.

Explain in a patient, unhurried voice what a lichen actually is, a partnership of fungus and alga living as a single organism, and why some patches on old gravestones grow so slowly that they can be used to date the stone beneath them.

Explain the ham sandwich theorem, which guarantees that a single straight slice can cut two pieces of bread and a slab of ham each exactly in half, no matter how carelessly they are scattered across the kitchen.

topic: Irrationality of the square root of two
prompt: Explain the classic proof that the square root of two cannot be written as a fraction, and why the discovery of such incommensurable lengths is said to have scandalized the Pythagoreans, who believed all things were number.

topic: first public demonstration of ether anesthesia
prompt: Write a vivid passage about the day in 1846 when ether anesthesia was first demonstrated publicly in a Boston operating theater, capturing the silence where screams had always been.

topic: Milky Way from a dark site
prompt: Describe, in the second person, seeing the Milky Way from a truly dark desert site for the first time, beneath a sky so clear that Venus casts a faint shadow on the sand.
Explain the McGurk effect, in which watching lips form 'ga' while hearing 'ba' makes people perceive a third sound, and what it reveals about how the brain fuses sight and sound.
Write a lyrical description of a double sunset on a planet orbiting two stars, like Kepler-16b, with twin shadows stretching from every object.

Explain why Britain and its colonies skipped eleven days in September 1752, when the 2nd of the month was followed directly by the 14th during the switch to the Gregorian calendar, and imagine what it felt like to wake up and find those days gone.
Describe an emperor penguin huddle during the Antarctic winter, as thousands of males balancing eggs on their feet shuffle in a slow rotation against the wind.

topic: Kibble balance and redefining the kilogram
prompt: Explain why, in 2019, scientists retired the metal cylinder that had defined the kilogram for over a century and redefined it in terms of Planck's constant using a device called the Kibble balance.

Explain the anthropological concept of liminality, the threshold stage of a rite of passage in which a person is no longer what they were and not yet what they will become, drawing on examples from initiation ceremonies to graduations.

Write a poignant passage about Georg Cantor's struggle to win acceptance for his theory of transfinite numbers in the face of Leopold Kronecker's fierce opposition and his own recurring bouts of depression.

Explain the concept of moral hazard, starting with a driver who becomes slightly more careless after buying comprehensive insurance and extending the idea to banks that expect to be rescued if their risky bets fail.

topic: Oort Cloud at solar system's edge
prompt: Write a lyrical description of the Oort Cloud, the vast and largely hypothetical shell of icy bodies marking the true outer edge of the solar system, from the viewpoint of a lonely comet nucleus drifting at its fringe.

topic: kilonovae and the origin of gold
prompt: Explain how much of the gold and platinum on Earth was likely forged in kilonovae, the cataclysmic collisions of neutron stars, writing as if addressing someone looking down at their own gold ring.

Explain how the Romans and medieval Europeans divided daylight into twelve hours that stretched long in summer and shrank in winter, and how the arrival of the mechanical clock turned this elastic time into rigid, equal hours.
Write a vivid description of the weather on the hot Jupiter HD 189733b, a cobalt-blue world where molten glass may rain sideways in winds of thousands of kilometres per hour.

Explain how Florence Nightingale used her colourful 'rose diagram' of Crimean War deaths to convince skeptical officials that far more soldiers were dying from preventable disease than from enemy fire.
Describe water droplets skittering and dancing across a very hot skillet, and the Leidenfrost effect that lets them hover on a cushion of their own vapour.
Write a brief story told from the perspective of a neutrophil racing through the bloodstream to a splinter wound, hunting bacteria before it sacrifices itself.

Explain Arthur Eddington's puzzle of the two tables, the solid, colored writing table of everyday life and the mostly empty swarm of particles described by physics, and ask which one is the real table.
Explain Occam's razor through the medical maxim 'when you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras,' and why simpler explanations deserve preference even though nature is not obliged to be simple.

topic: restoring ruins or letting them decay
prompt: Argue whether old ruins should be restored to their former glory or left to crumble gracefully, weighing John Ruskin's conviction that restoration is a kind of lie against the case for rebuilding what was lost.

topic: Red Queen hypothesis and why sex exists
prompt: Explain the Red Queen hypothesis, which proposes that sexual reproduction persists because organisms must keep shuffling their genes just to stay ahead of evolving parasites, drawing on Lewis Carroll's image of running just to stand still.

Write a lyrical description of the tip-of-the-tongue state, capturing the maddening feeling of a word that hovers just out of reach, its first letter and rhythm known while the whole refuses to surface.
Describe, as though you were standing beside him, how Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth by comparing the shadow of a stick in Alexandria with the sunlit bottom of a well in Syene.

Write a brief story in which Karl Schwarzschild, serving as an artillery officer on the Russian front in 1915, works out the first exact solution to Einstein's field equations and mails it to Einstein.
Write a lyrical description of a starling murmuration at dusk, conveying how thousands of birds wheel as one while each follows only its nearest neighbors.

Compare how the Müller-Lyer illusion affects people raised in rectangular, 'carpentered' cities versus foraging peoples of the Kalahari, and what the contrast suggests about whether visual perception is learned.

topic: Pigeonhole principle and hairs on heads
prompt: Explain the pigeonhole principle and how this almost childishly simple idea proves that at least two people in London have exactly the same number of hairs on their heads.

topic: Phineas Gage and the frontal lobes
prompt: Explain what the 1848 accident of Phineas Gage, the railroad foreman who survived an iron rod driven clean through his skull, taught early scientists about the frontal lobes and personality.

topic: Ada Lovelace and the Analytical Engine
prompt: Explain, for a reader who has never written a line of code, what Ada Lovelace saw in Charles Babbage's never-built Analytical Engine that even Babbage had not fully grasped: that a machine manipulating numbers might also compose music or handle any kind of symbol.

topic: Darwin's orchid and the predicted moth
prompt: Explain how Charles Darwin, examining a Madagascar orchid with a nectar spur nearly a foot long, predicted the existence of a moth with an equally long tongue decades before it was found.
Explain Wittgenstein's beetle-in-a-box analogy, in which everyone has a box no one else can look into, and what it implies about how words for private sensations like pain get their meaning.

Explain Emmy Noether's theorem, which ties every continuous symmetry of nature to a conserved quantity such as energy or momentum, and why physicists consider it one of the most profound results of the twentieth century.
Explain Newton's cannonball thought experiment, beginning with the image of a cannon on an impossibly tall mountain, and show how a shot fired fast enough falls around the Earth forever.

Write a vivid description of the final minutes before a summer thunderstorm breaks, capturing the sudden drop in pressure, the sharp metallic smell of ozone, the leaves flipping to show their pale undersides and the hush before the first crack of thunder.

topic: diel vertical migration in the ocean
prompt: Explain diel vertical migration, the largest daily movement of animals on Earth, as countless small creatures rise from the deep ocean each night to feed and sink back down before dawn.
Explain inattentional blindness through the famous experiment in which viewers busy counting basketball passes completely fail to notice a person in a gorilla suit strolling through the scene.

Explain Ernest Rutherford's gold foil experiment and why the rare alpha particles bouncing straight back struck him as being as incredible as a fifteen-inch shell rebounding off a sheet of tissue paper.
Explain the mirror self-recognition test, which animals have passed it, and why a positive result for a small cleaner fish sparked debate about what the test really measures.
Write a lyrical description of Smale's sphere eversion, the astonishing discovery that a sphere can be turned completely inside out without tearing or creasing, as long as it may pass through itself.

Explain pareidolia, the brain's habit of seeing faces in clouds, electrical sockets and the front grilles of cars, to a curious teenager, and suggest why evolution might have favoured such a jumpy face detector.

Explain Conway's law, the observation that organizations inevitably design systems that mirror their own communication structures, using the wry example that four teams building a compiler will produce a four-pass compiler.

Describe Galileo's cold nights in January 1610 as he trained his homemade telescope on Jupiter and watched four tiny points of light shift from night to night, until he understood that they were moons circling another world.

Using the metaphor of a city that breathed water, describe sunrise over twelfth-century Angkor, when Angkor Wat stood at the heart of a vast engineered landscape of reservoirs, canals and rice fields sustaining perhaps the largest pre-industrial city on Earth.

topic: security through obscurity vs Kerckhoffs's principle
prompt: Argue whether 'security through obscurity' ever has a legitimate place, weighing it against Kerckhoffs's principle that a cryptosystem should stay secure even if everything about it except the key becomes public.
Explain the Jain doctrine of anekantavada, or many-sidedness, through the parable of the blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and argue about what it is.
Explain how radiocarbon dating works, from cosmic rays creating carbon-14 in the upper atmosphere to the steady ticking of its half-life inside ancient bones and wood.
Write a vivid, sensory description of experiencing a total solar eclipse, from the eerie sharpening of shadows and the sudden chill to the blooming of the pearly corona.

topic: choanoflagellates and the origin of animals
prompt: Explain why choanoflagellates, single-celled organisms that sometimes form colonies, are considered the closest living relatives of animals and what they reveal about how animal life began.
Write a lyrical description of the green flash, the brief emerald spark that can appear at the top of the Sun just as it vanishes below a clear sea horizon.
Write a short reflective passage about the dodo, which lived without predators on Mauritius and vanished within a century of human arrival.

Explain why a soap bubble swirls with shifting rainbow colours, describing how light reflecting from the inner and outer surfaces of a film thinner than a wavelength interferes with itself, in the voice of someone watching a child blow bubbles in a garden.

Explain the 'coffee ring effect', why a spilled drop of coffee dries into a dark ring rather than an even stain as liquid rushes outward and carries particles to the edge, treating the ring as a small accidental artwork left on a café table.

topic: dung beetles navigating by the Milky Way
prompt: Explain how dung beetles roll their balls in straight lines by orienting to the glow of the Milky Way, making them the first animals known to navigate by the galaxy.

topic: running across a pool of oobleck
prompt: Describe what it feels like to run across a pool of oobleck, a cornstarch-and-water mixture that firms up under each pounding step but swallows you if you stand still.

Explain why a dry stick of spaghetti bent from both ends almost never breaks into just two pieces, a puzzle that once intrigued Richard Feynman, and how twisting it first finally makes it snap cleanly in two.

Describe the moment in Seoul in 2016 when AlphaGo played its now-famous 'Move 37' against Lee Sedol, capturing how commentators first took it for a blunder before realizing they had witnessed a move no human would have dared to play.
Write a lyrical description of the Pythagorean idea of the music of the spheres, in which the planets hum in mathematical harmonies so constant that human ears have never noticed them.

topic: Last day of Ötzi the Iceman
prompt: Write a vivid reconstruction of the last day of Ötzi the Iceman, the 5,300-year-old man found in an Alpine glacier, drawing on clues from his final meal, his copper axe, his unfinished arrows and the arrowhead lodged in his shoulder.
Explain how a siphon lifts liquid up and over an obstacle, and why physicists still argue over whether gravity or atmospheric pressure deserves the credit.
Write a brief story in which a hiker in a remote Australian canyon stumbles upon a grove of trees that were thought to have vanished alongside the dinosaurs.

topic: hydraulic jump in a kitchen sink
prompt: Explain the hydraulic jump, the circular ring that forms where water from a tap spreads across the bottom of a sink and suddenly thickens, and how it relates to the tidal bores that surge up great rivers.

Explain Cantor's diagonal argument and why it proves there are more real numbers than whole numbers, walking the reader through the trick of building a number that differs from every entry on any supposedly complete list.

Write a passage explaining why ancient Roman concrete has survived two thousand years in harbors and domes while modern concrete cracks within decades, including the discovery of lime clasts that let it heal its own cracks.

Explain how planets grow from microscopic grains of dust in a young star's disk, including the puzzling 'metre-size barrier' at which growing pebbles should spiral into the star before they can become planets.
Argue whether laws against price gouging after natural disasters protect vulnerable people or end up worsening shortages by blunting the price signals that draw supplies into stricken areas.

topic: Lady Lovelace's objection to machine originality
prompt: Take a position on Ada Lovelace's famous objection that the Analytical Engine can only do whatever we know how to order it to perform, and argue whether today's AI systems have proved her right or wrong.
Explain the surprisingly unsettled science of why ice is slippery, and why the old textbook story that a skate blade melts the ice by pressure does not hold up.
Explain how a date palm seed recovered from the ruins of Masada, roughly two thousand years old, was coaxed into germinating, and what that reveals about seed dormancy.

Describe the night during the siege of Constantinople in 1453 when Ottoman soldiers hauled dozens of warships over a hill on greased wooden rails to slip past the great chain guarding the Golden Horn.
Explain phage therapy, the century-old idea of using viruses that infect only bacteria to cure infections, and why it is being revived as antibiotics fail.

Explain John Locke's experiment of warming one hand and chilling the other before plunging both into the same lukewarm water, and how it supports his distinction between primary and secondary qualities.

Write a tender description of a kitchen doorframe marked with pencil lines and dates recording children's heights over many years, as seen on the day the family carries out the last box and moves away.

topic: Hubble tension new physics or error
prompt: Argue whether the 'Hubble tension,' the stubborn disagreement between different measurements of how fast the universe is expanding, is more likely to signal new physics or an undiscovered measurement error.

Write a lyrical description of a bowl of fruit on a kitchen table over the course of one week as it ripens, softens and finally decays, in the spirit of a seventeenth-century Dutch vanitas still life.
Explain why the viral 2015 photograph of 'the dress' split viewers between blue-and-black and white-and-gold, focusing on the brain's unconscious assumptions about lighting and color constancy.

topic: wildlife of the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone
prompt: Describe the forests and abandoned streets of the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone today, where wolves, wild horses and bison roam in the absence of people.
Write a vivid passage about the great Leonid meteor storm of November 1833, when tens of thousands of shooting stars an hour woke and frightened people across North America.
Explain Harry Frankfurt's distinction between a liar and a bullshitter, and why he thought indifference to the truth is more corrosive than deliberately denying it.
Describe what it would be like to be Ireneo Funes from Borges' story, a man who forgets nothing and is therefore barely able to think, because thinking requires forgetting differences.
Argue whether an artificial intelligence that behaved in every way as if it suffered would deserve moral consideration, even if we could never be sure it felt anything.
Write a story in which a 1920s light-bulb engineer is ordered by the Phoebus cartel to make bulbs that burn out after 1,000 hours, and must wrestle with designing failure into his own invention.
Explain how cuttlefish change color and skin texture in a fraction of a second to blend into their surroundings, even though they appear to be color-blind.

Explain how the Comte de Buffon showed that randomly dropping needles onto a floor of parallel boards can be used to estimate the value of pi, and why a circle's constant turns up in a problem about straight lines.
Explain generative adversarial networks through the image of an art forger and a detective locked in an escalating contest, each improving only because the other keeps getting better.

Write a short reflective passage about the screeching, warbling handshake of a dial-up modem, evoking both the nostalgia of the sound and what the two machines were actually negotiating as they 'sang' to each other.

Explain the philosophical argument of Dostoevsky's parable of the Grand Inquisitor, who tells a returned Christ that humanity cannot bear the burden of freedom and longs instead for bread, miracle, mystery and authority.
Explain what brown dwarfs are, objects too massive to be planets but too small to sustain hydrogen fusion, and why they are often called 'failed stars.'
Write a short reflective passage about the Hubble Deep Field, in which astronomers aimed the telescope for days at a seemingly empty speck of sky and found it crowded with thousands of galaxies.

Explain why the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... grows without limit despite its ever-shrinking terms, and how this lets you stack identical books at the edge of a table so the top one overhangs as far as you like.

topic: warning future humans about nuclear waste
prompt: Explain the problem facing the designers of Finland's Onkalo nuclear waste repository: how to warn people a hundred thousand years from now, who may share none of our languages or symbols, never to dig there.
Write a lyrical description of a total lunar eclipse, conveying that the Moon's copper-red glow is the light of every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once.

topic: Brahmagupta and the invention of zero
prompt: Explain to a curious teenager how zero grew from a humble placeholder dot into a true number with its own rules in the work of the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta, and why 'nothing' turned out to be one of humanity's greatest ideas.

topic: Central limit theorem and bell curves
prompt: Explain the central limit theorem through an everyday analogy, showing why adding up many small, independent random nudges so reliably produces the familiar bell-shaped curve, whatever the nudges look like individually.

Describe a bustling medieval trade fair in the Champagne region of France, where merchants from Italy and Flanders met to trade cloth, spices and written promises of payment, giving birth to early forms of credit.
Explain the puzzle of the 'Methuselah star' HD 140283, whose age was first estimated to be greater than that of the universe itself, and how astronomers resolved the apparent contradiction.

topic: free diving and the dive reflex
prompt: Describe what it would be like to free dive into deep blue water on a single breath, as the mammalian dive reflex slows the heart, the light from the surface fades and the body begins to sink without effort.
Using the analogy of a car's speedometer and odometer, explain the fundamental theorem of calculus and why the slope of a curve and the area beneath it turn out to be two sides of the same coin.
Write a reflective passage about how tuberculosis, known as consumption, was romanticized in the nineteenth century as a disease of poets and artists, before the bacterium behind it was identified.
Explain the holographic principle, the idea that all the information inside a region of space might be encoded on its boundary, like a three-dimensional image stored on a flat hologram.
Compare chimpanzees and bonobos, our two closest living relatives, in how they resolve conflict and organize their societies, and reflect on what each suggests about human nature.

topic: Y2K bug: hype or quiet triumph
prompt: Argue whether the Y2K millennium bug was an overblown panic or a genuine disaster quietly averted by years of unglamorous work by programmers.

topic: journey of a red blood cell
prompt: Describe the journey of a single red blood cell as it squeezes through capillaries, picks up oxygen in the lungs and returns to the heart, written as a vivid travelogue.
Argue whether Socrates was right that the unexamined life is not worth living, or whether a life of unreflective contentment can be just as good.
Explain the optimal stopping strategy known as the secretary problem, or the 37 percent rule, and half-seriously apply it to someone trying to decide when to stop viewing apartments and sign a lease.

Write an engaging explanation of how MP3 compression shrinks music by discarding sounds the human ear cannot perceive, such as quiet tones masked by louder ones close in pitch, so that most of the data vanishes without listeners noticing.

Describe Tenochtitlan as Spanish soldiers first saw it in 1519, an island city of causeways, canals, floating chinampa gardens and gleaming temples rising from Lake Texcoco, which some of them compared to an enchanted vision from a romance.

Write a short reflective passage imagining Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's astonishment as he peered through his tiny handmade lens at a drop of rainwater and became the first person ever to see it teeming with living 'animalcules'.

topic: Routley's last man and nature's value
prompt: Argue whether the last person alive on Earth would be doing anything wrong by destroying a forest on their final day, and what the answer reveals about whether nature has value in itself.

Explain Kolmogorov complexity, the idea that the true information content of something is the length of the shortest program that could produce it, opening with the question of whether a million zeros or a million random coin flips is more 'complex.'

Describe what it would be like to climb the narrow stairs between the two shells of Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, seeing up close the herringbone brickwork that let the largest masonry dome in the world rise without wooden scaffolding beneath it.
Explain why the far side of the Moon is not actually dark, and why its rugged, crater-packed face looks so different from the familiar near side.

Explain how thousands of fireflies in the Great Smoky Mountains come to flash in near-perfect unison each June with no conductor directing them, in a passage that reads like the description of an orchestra tuning itself in the dark.
Explain how Giuseppe Peano constructed a continuous curve that passes through every single point of a square, and why such a 'monster' unsettled mathematicians' intuitions about what dimension means.
Explain how a handclap at the foot of the stepped pyramid of El Castillo at Chichén Itzá returns as a descending chirp that some have likened to the call of the sacred quetzal bird.
Describe the Laetoli footprints, left about 3.6 million years ago by upright-walking hominins crossing fresh volcanic ash in what is now Tanzania, imagining the moment they were made.

topic: Galvani versus Volta over frog legs
prompt: Explain the scientific quarrel between Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta over why dissected frog legs twitched when touched with metal, and how their dispute gave the world both the electric battery and the study of nerve signals.

Using the metaphor of a nervous system stretched across a continent, explain how the Mongol Empire's Yam network of relay stations, fresh horses and riders carried messages across Eurasia at astonishing speed, and how a metal tablet called a paiza served as a traveler's passport.
Argue whether learning to cook food over fire was the decisive step that made us human, as the cooking hypothesis proposes.
Explain the theory that Viking navigators used 'sunstones,' crystals of Iceland spar, to find the Sun's position through clouds by detecting the polarization of skylight.

Write a reflective passage on Pascal's claim that humanity's troubles stem from our inability to sit quietly alone in a room, imagining what a person is fleeing from each time they reach for a diversion.

Explain fully homomorphic encryption using the metaphor of a locked glovebox in which a jeweler can craft a ring without ever touching or seeing the gold, just as a cloud server can compute on data it can never read.
Explain Newton's rotating bucket argument and why the curved surface of spinning water puzzled thinkers from Newton to Ernst Mach to Einstein about what rotation is really relative to.

Describe, in vivid prose, what an observer sees when liquid helium is cooled to about two degrees above absolute zero and suddenly stops boiling, then begins creeping up and over the walls of its container as a frictionless superfluid.
Argue for or against the 'block universe' view, which holds that past, present and future are equally real and that the flowing 'now' we experience is an illusion.

topic: tsunami speed in the deep ocean
prompt: Explain why a tsunami can cross the deep ocean as fast as a jet airliner while being barely noticeable to ships, and why it rears up into a towering wall only as it reaches shallow coastal water.
Write a short reflective passage about Heinrich Hertz's remark that the electromagnetic waves he had just produced in his laboratory were of no use whatsoever.
Explain how the 'immortal jellyfish' Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from its adult form to a juvenile stage when stressed, potentially repeating its life cycle indefinitely.
Describe what it would be like to lose your sense of proprioception overnight, so that you could only know where your limbs were by looking at them.
Write a lyrical description of the zodiacal light, the faint, tilted cone of glow that rises from the horizon before dawn, made by sunlight scattering off dust between the planets.

topic: pitcher plant as tree shrew toilet
prompt: Explain how a Bornean pitcher plant has evolved to serve as a toilet for tree shrews, collecting their droppings as fertilizer rather than relying on trapped insects.

Describe the discovery of the first pulsar in 1967, when a graduate student noticed a bit of 'scruff' on a long strip of chart paper, a signal so regular it was half-jokingly labelled LGM-1, for 'little green men.'

topic: locust transformation from solitary to swarming
prompt: Explain how a solitary desert grasshopper transforms into a gregarious swarming locust when crowded, changing its color, its behaviour and even the size of its brain.
Argue whether the dead can be wronged, for example by breaking a deathbed promise or slandering someone long after they are gone, even though they will never know.

Explain Clark and Chalmers' extended mind thesis through the story of Otto, a man with memory loss who relies on a notebook to find his way to a museum, and whether that notebook is literally part of his mind.

Explain how Cecilia Payne, in her 1925 doctoral thesis, showed that stars are made overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium, a conclusion so contrary to accepted belief that she was persuaded to call it 'almost certainly not real.'

Write a short, mind-bending piece explaining Thomson's lamp, a lamp switched on and off infinitely many times within two minutes, and why asking whether it is on or off at the end exposes deep puzzles about completing infinite tasks.
Write an evocative passage describing the autumn of 1918, when a new strain of influenza swept the world and struck down healthy young adults with frightening speed.

topic: Aristotle's sea battle and future contingents
prompt: Explain Aristotle's puzzle about tomorrow's sea battle: if it is already true today that a battle will happen tomorrow, does that make the future fixed and our deliberation pointless?

Explain the Kepler conjecture about the densest way to stack cannonballs, and why a fact every greengrocer piling oranges already seemed to know took nearly four centuries and a massive computer-assisted proof to settle.
Write a playful, reflective passage about the experience of an earworm, a song fragment that loops endlessly in the mind, weaving in what is known about why certain tunes get stuck.

Describe the atmosphere of the 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels, where Einstein would arrive at breakfast with a new thought experiment to undermine quantum theory and Bohr would have a rebuttal ready by dinner.
Write a lyrical description of the swirling colours on a soap bubble, explaining how they arise from light interfering within a film thinner than a wavelength.

Describe the scene Sartre imagines of a person peering through a keyhole, utterly absorbed, who suddenly hears footsteps in the hall and is flooded with shame at being seen, as an illustration of how the gaze of others shapes who we are.
Write a brief story about the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa from the Louvre, told from the perspective of the handyman who walked out of the museum with the painting hidden under his smock.
Write a reflective passage about the ginkgo trees that survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and still grow there, remembering that ginkgos as a lineage have outlasted the dinosaurs.

Describe the predawn moment of the Trinity test in the New Mexico desert in July 1945, conveying the impossible light, the wave of heat, the delayed thunder and the uneasy silence among the scientists who watched.

Explain how Claude Chappe's optical telegraph, a chain of hilltop towers with pivoting wooden arms, could carry messages across revolutionary France in minutes, half a century before the electric telegraph.
Explain the hairy ball theorem—why you can never comb a hairy coconut flat without leaving a cowlick—and why it guarantees that somewhere on Earth the wind is not blowing at all.

topic: Euler's solution of the Basel problem
prompt: Explain how the young Leonhard Euler solved the Basel problem, showing that the sum of the reciprocals of the square numbers equals π²/6, and why finding pi in a problem with no circles in sight caused such a sensation.

Write a short reflective passage imagining Marcus Aurelius writing his private Meditations by lamplight in a cold military camp on the Danube frontier, the most powerful man in the world reminding himself to be humble, patient and kind.

Write a reflective passage about Point Nemo, the oceanic pole of inaccessibility so remote that the nearest humans are often astronauts passing overhead, and where retired spacecraft are sent to sink.

Write a brief story in which swift Achilles races a tortoise that has been given a head start and slowly realizes, as Zeno argued, that each time he reaches where the tortoise was, it has crept a little further ahead.

Explain the decoy effect using the magazine subscription experiment in which adding an unattractive print-only option, priced the same as print plus web, dramatically shifted buyers toward the combined deal.

Write an evocative passage on Kierkegaard's claim that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom, using the image of someone at the edge of a cliff who feels not only the fear of falling but the terrifying possibility of jumping.

Write a calm, meditative passage explaining the Japanese practice of shinrin-yoku, or 'forest bathing', and the research suggesting that unhurried time among trees can lower stress hormones, heart rate and blood pressure.
Explain gamma-ray bursts, the most luminous explosions in the universe, and the irony that they were first detected by satellites built to watch for secret nuclear weapons tests.
Write a brief story in which a volunteer astronomer in 1977, poring over computer printouts from the Big Ear radio telescope, circles a strange sequence of characters and writes 'Wow!' in the margin.
Explain the placebo effect, including the surprising findings that larger pills, pricier pills and even placebos given openly as placebos can produce measurable relief.

topic: Plato's charioteer allegory of the soul
prompt: Describe Plato's allegory from the Phaedrus of the soul as a charioteer driving two winged horses, one noble and one unruly, in vivid, dramatic prose.
Argue whether the legend that Archimedes set Roman warships ablaze with mirrors during the siege of Syracuse could have been physically possible.

Write a lyrical description of Great Zimbabwe at its height in the fourteenth century, imagining the sweeping granite walls of the Great Enclosure and the traders arriving with gold, ivory and Chinese porcelain.
Explain the counterintuitive rule of orbital mechanics that to catch up with a spacecraft ahead of you in the same orbit, you must first fire your engines backwards and slow down.

Argue for or against G.H. Hardy's proud claim that the purest mathematics is valuable precisely because it is useless, considering that his beloved number theory later became a backbone of internet security.
Explain the 'windshield phenomenon,' the observation that car windshields no longer get splattered with insects as they did decades ago, and what scientists have found about the decline of insects.
Argue whether Brutalist architecture, with its massive forms of raw concrete, is an ugly relic that should be demolished or an honest and heroic style worth preserving.
Take a position on whether photographing every beautiful moment on a phone diminishes our ability to truly experience and remember it, and defend that position with feeling.

Explain the idea that dopamine signals not pleasure itself but the gap between expected and actual reward, illustrated by the monkey experiments in which neurons came to fire at a predictive light rather than at the juice.

topic: Turing machine and its endless tape
prompt: Write a meditative description of a Turing machine at work, its reading head inching back and forth along an endless paper tape one symbol at a time, and yet capable in principle of any computation a modern supercomputer can perform.

Explain how a gravity assist works, showing how a spacecraft can steal a little of a planet's orbital momentum to speed up, using the image of a tennis ball bouncing off the front of an oncoming train.

Explain William Paley's watchmaker argument, which begins with stumbling upon a watch lying on a heath, and how Darwin's theory of natural selection offered a way to get design-like order without a designer.
In a light, reassuring tone, explain the friendship paradox—why, on average, your friends have more friends than you do—to someone who suspects everyone else is simply more popular.
Explain how metamaterials, engineered structures with properties not found in nature, can steer light around an object and make invisibility cloaks a real, if limited, possibility.
Describe the Philae lander's improbable touchdown on comet 67P in 2014, bouncing twice across the surface in the comet's feeble gravity before coming to rest in shadow beside a cliff.
Explain why we still divide hours into sixty minutes and circles into 360 degrees, tracing these habits back to the Babylonian base-60 number system and the practical advantages that made it endure.
Explain why the tritone earned the nickname 'diabolus in musica', what makes this interval sound so restless and unresolved, and how it later became essential to blues, jazz and heavy metal.
Explain why flashbulb memories of shocking public events feel vividly certain yet drift dramatically over the years, as studies of people's recollections of the Challenger disaster revealed.

Explain differential privacy for a reader who has never written a line of code, showing how adding carefully calibrated random noise to statistics lets a census learn about a population without revealing anything about any single person in it.

topic: a crow that remembers a face
prompt: Write a brief story about a crow who remembers the face of a person who once trapped it and, years later, leads its whole family to scold that person in the street.

topic: a seed from the Svalbard vault
prompt: Write a brief story set centuries in the future, in which a child plants a seed retrieved from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault and grows a crop that no one alive has ever tasted.
Explain al-Ghazali's example of cotton brought into contact with fire, and his argument that we never actually observe the fire causing the burning, only one event regularly accompanying another.
Explain how bee orchids deceive male bees by mimicking the look, feel and scent of a female, tricking them into carrying pollen without offering any reward.

topic: diffusion models denoising static into images
prompt: Write a lyrical description of how an AI diffusion model creates a picture, starting from pure television static and removing noise step by step until a recognizable scene emerges, like a photograph slowly developing in a darkroom tray.

Argue whether a person who was as morally good as possible in every action would be someone to admire, or whether, as Susan Wolf suggested, such a moral saint would lack something essential to a good life.

topic: Harvard Mark II moth, first bug
prompt: Write a vivid scene describing the day in 1947 when operators of the Harvard Mark II computer found a moth trapped in one of its relays and taped it into the logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found.'

Explain how thousands of starlings in a murmuration move as a single rippling shape without any leader, each bird responding only to its nearest handful of neighbours, in prose that captures the wonder of watching it over a marsh at dusk.

topic: cosmic ray bit flips in memory
prompt: Explain how high-energy particles from space can flip a single bit inside a computer's memory, referencing the 2003 Belgian election in which one candidate inexplicably gained exactly 4,096 extra votes, and how engineers guard against such invisible strikes.

topic: axial tilt as cause of seasons
prompt: Explain why Earth has seasons, gently correcting the widespread belief that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
Describe how, in 1932, Bell Labs engineer Karl Jansky, hunting for sources of static that troubled transatlantic telephone calls, found a faint hiss coming from the center of the Milky Way.

topic: Buridan's ass and perfectly balanced choice
prompt: Explain the puzzle of Buridan's ass, the perfectly rational donkey that starves between two identical bales of hay, and what it reveals about choosing when reasons are perfectly balanced.

topic: Pando, the aspen that is one organism
prompt: Write a lyrical description of walking through Pando in Utah, a grove of tens of thousands of quaking aspens that are all one organism sharing a single ancient root system, while its leaves tremble gold in the autumn wind.

Explain digital steganography, the art of hiding a secret message inside an ordinary-looking photograph by subtly altering the least significant bits of its pixels, and how its goal differs from that of encryption.
Write a reflective passage about Pando, the grove of quaking aspen in Utah that is actually a single organism with tens of thousands of trunks sharing one root system.

Explain the 'Great Dimming' of Betelgeuse in 2019–2020, when the red supergiant faded noticeably and fuelled speculation that it was about to explode, and what astronomers concluded had actually happened.

Explain how Henrietta Swan Leavitt, working as a poorly paid human 'computer' at Harvard Observatory, discovered that the pulsing rhythm of certain stars reveals their true brightness, giving astronomers their first yardstick for measuring the universe.

Explain the geological theory that the trances of the Pythia, the priestess of the Oracle at Delphi, were induced by sweet-smelling gases rising from fault lines beneath Apollo's temple, and why the idea is still debated.

topic: starlight as a message from the past
prompt: Explain why looking up at the night sky is really looking into the past, since the light reaching your eyes from some stars set out before your great-grandparents were born, in a tone of quiet astonishment.
Describe what happens inside a chrysalis as a caterpillar dissolves much of its body into a soup of cells and rebuilds itself as a butterfly.

Write an explanatory passage about hemispatial neglect, the condition in which a stroke patient may eat only the right half of their plate and draw clocks with all twelve numbers crowded onto one side.

topic: Inge Lehmann and Earth's inner core
prompt: Explain how the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann, studying faint seismic waves from a 1929 earthquake, deduced in 1936 that Earth has a solid inner core hidden within its liquid outer core.

Explain how the first message sent over ARPANET in October 1969 was supposed to read 'LOGIN' but crashed the system after two letters, and how the idea of packet switching made the network that grew into the internet possible.

Explain how group theory describes the Rubik's Cube and how mathematicians proved that every one of its 43 quintillion scrambled positions can be solved in twenty moves or fewer, a figure nicknamed 'God's number.'

Explain the Gale–Shapley stable matching algorithm, why it always produces pairings in which no two people would both rather abandon their partners for each other, and how a version of it now matches new doctors to hospitals.
Explain the incongruity theory of humor, associated with thinkers like Kant and Schopenhauer, showing how laughter springs from the sudden collapse of an expectation into something absurd.
Explain the phenomenon of ant mills, in which army ants blindly following pheromone trails can become trapped in a circling death spiral, and what it reveals about the limits of simple rules.

topic: Epictetus and the Stoic dichotomy of control
prompt: Explain the Stoic dichotomy of control as taught by Epictetus, a philosopher who had once been enslaved, and how separating what is up to us from what is not was meant to make a person unshakable.
Write a short reflective passage about kintsugi, the Japanese art of mending broken pottery with gold-dusted lacquer, using it as a metaphor for how people carry their own repaired fractures.
Describe, in the second person, standing on a misty mountain ridge with the Sun at your back and seeing your own giant shadow cast on the clouds, ringed by a rainbow halo called a glory.
Describe what it would be like to climb Olympus Mons on Mars, a volcano so vast and gently sloped that its summit would lie beyond the horizon for someone standing at its base.
Explain who 'Mitochondrial Eve' was and why she was neither the first woman nor the only woman alive in her time.

topic: perceiving the world by bat echolocation
prompt: Describe what it would be like to perceive the world through echolocation as a bat, hunting moths in the dark by listening to the shapes of returning echoes.

Explain Hannah Arendt's phrase 'the banality of evil,' coined while she observed the trial of Adolf Eichmann, and why her suggestion that great harm can flow from thoughtless obedience unsettled so many readers.
Write a lyrical monologue in the voice of an old manual typewriter gathering dust in an attic, which remembers every love letter, unfinished novel and rejection notice it ever struck onto paper.
Explain why comets often show two distinct tails, one of dust and one of ions, and why both point away from the Sun even when the comet is heading outward.
Explain to a curious ten-year-old why you get a little electric shock when you touch a doorknob after shuffling across a carpet, especially on dry winter days.

topic: Galois's final night before the duel
prompt: Write an evocative passage imagining the night before twenty-year-old Évariste Galois's fatal duel in 1832, as he hurriedly scrawled his mathematical ideas into a final letter to a friend.
Describe the moment in 1923 when Edwin Hubble, studying a photographic plate of the Andromeda 'nebula,' crossed out an 'N' and scrawled 'VAR!', realizing it was a whole galaxy far beyond our own.
Describe what Earth might have looked like during a Snowball Earth episode, when ice may have reached nearly to the equator and life clung on in hidden refuges.
Describe Welwitschia mirabilis in the Namib Desert, a plant that grows only two leaves in its entire life of a thousand years or more, letting them fray into ribbons across the sand.

Explain why Jeremy Bentham insisted that the question about animals is not whether they can reason or talk but whether they can suffer, and how this reframing reshaped moral thinking about other species.

topic: how general anesthesia switches off consciousness
prompt: Explain what scientists currently understand about how general anesthesia switches off consciousness, and why it remains remarkable that doctors can reliably make a mind vanish and return without fully knowing how.

topic: St. Elmo's fire on ship masts
prompt: Describe the eerie blue-violet glow of St. Elmo's fire crackling on the masts of a sailing ship during a storm, and the physics of electrical discharge behind it.
Write a short story about Johannes Kepler's years-long 'war with Mars,' ending at the moment he realizes the planet's orbit is not a circle but an ellipse.
Explain Braess's paradox, in which adding a new road to a network can make every driver's journey slower, and describe how closing roads in some real cities has actually eased congestion.

Explain Maxwell's demon as if introducing a mischievous character in a fable, describing the tiny being that sorts fast and slow molecules to seemingly defeat the second law of thermodynamics, and why erasing its memory ultimately foils it.

topic: bubble sort performed as folk dance
prompt: Write a playful description of a troupe of folk dancers performing a bubble sort, swapping places pair by pair until the line stands in perfect numerical order, conveying both the charm and the comic inefficiency of the algorithm.

Describe the Christmas Truce of 1914, when British and German soldiers along the Western Front climbed out of their frozen trenches to sing carols, trade cigarettes and kick a football across no man's land.

Explain reward hacking, or specification gaming, in reinforcement learning, using the famous example of an AI boat-racing agent that learned to spin in endless circles collecting points instead of ever finishing the race.

topic: lessons of the cold fusion affair
prompt: Argue whether the 1989 cold fusion announcement, in which two chemists claimed to have produced nuclear fusion in a tabletop cell, should be remembered as an embarrassment for science or as proof that its self-correcting machinery works.

Write a lyrical description of Machu Picchu at dawn as the clouds lift from the surrounding peaks, lingering on the Inca stone walls fitted together so precisely, without mortar, that not even a knife blade can slip between them.
Argue whether Albert Einstein deserves the lion's share of credit for special relativity, given that Hendrik Lorentz and Henri Poincaré had already worked out much of its mathematics.
Explain how stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbial mats, preserve some of the oldest evidence of life on Earth and still grow today in Shark Bay, Australia.
Write a calm, reflective passage on Lucretius' symmetry argument: since we feel no distress at the eternity that passed before we were born, why should we fear the eternity that follows our death?

Explain the Michelson–Morley experiment of 1887, which searched for the 'aether wind' through which light was supposed to travel, and why its null result is often called the most important failed experiment in physics.

Explain the quantum Zeno effect, the strange prediction, since confirmed in the laboratory, that repeatedly observing an unstable quantum system can freeze it in place, like a watched pot that truly never boils.

topic: white holes as reversed black holes
prompt: Explain what a white hole is, the time-reversed twin of a black hole that nothing can ever enter, and why physicists debate whether such objects could exist in nature.

Describe how Christiaan Huygens, sick in bed in 1665, noticed that two pendulum clocks hanging from the same beam had mysteriously fallen into step with each other, which he called an 'odd kind of sympathy.'

Write a lyrical description, opening with the words 'Every ruin was once someone's present,' of the strange pleasure people have long taken in ruins, from ivy on broken arches to roofless abbeys open to the sky.
Explain how a falling cat manages to turn itself over and land on its feet with nothing to push against, a puzzle that once seemed to defy the conservation of angular momentum.

Explain what historians know and still debate about Greek fire, the Byzantine weapon that kept burning even on water, and how its formula was guarded so jealously that it was eventually lost to history.

topic: Rubber hand illusion and bodily self
prompt: Describe what it feels like to experience the rubber hand illusion, when a fake hand stroked in sync with your hidden real one suddenly feels like your own, and what it reveals about how fragile our sense of the body is.

topic: why scratching an itch feels good
prompt: Explain why scratching an itch feels so satisfying, including how the mild pain of scratching temporarily silences itch signals in the spinal cord.

topic: Pompeii on the morning of eruption
prompt: Describe the day Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE through the eyes of a Pompeii baker sliding the morning's loaves into his oven as a strange, pine-shaped cloud begins to rise over the mountain.

Explain what it would mean for pi to be a 'normal' number, and why, despite trillions of computed digits, nobody can yet prove that every finite string of digits, such as your phone number, must appear somewhere in its expansion.
Describe, from the perspective of the prisoner in Plato's cave who is dragged up into the sunlight, the pain, confusion and slow wonder of seeing real things for the first time.
Explain why certain moments in music can send a shiver down the spine, exploring what happens in the brain's reward system during musical frisson.
Write a lyrical description of the date-due slip glued inside an old library book, its column of stamped dates stretching back decades, imagining the strangers who each carried the same story home.
Explain how ultramarine, the luminous blue pigment ground from Afghan lapis lazuli, came to cost more than gold in Renaissance Europe, and why painters reserved it for the robes of the Virgin Mary.

topic: packing two meters of DNA into a nucleus
prompt: Explain how about two meters of DNA is packed into a cell nucleus only a few millionths of a meter across, using the analogy of thread wound onto spools.

topic: myth of flowing medieval window glass
prompt: Argue against the persistent myth that old cathedral windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is a slowly flowing liquid, making the case for what glass really is.
Write a brief story retelling Archimedes' 'Eureka!' moment, in which a king's suspicion about a golden crown leads him to the principle of buoyancy in the public baths.
Explain how the fourth-century Roman Lycurgus Cup glows jade green in reflected light but blood red when lit from within, and how its glassmakers unknowingly practiced a kind of nanotechnology.

Write a vivid sensory description of a Phoenician dye works in ancient Tyre, where heaps of crushed murex sea snails rotted in vats to produce the foul-smelling but priceless purple worn by kings and emperors.
Argue whether the Western Roman Empire truly 'fell' in 476 CE, or whether it is more accurate to say it gradually transformed into the kingdoms of early medieval Europe.

topic: Correspondence versus coherence theories of truth
prompt: Compare the correspondence and coherence theories of truth, using the image of a map judged either by how well it matches the land or by how consistently it fits with all the other maps we trust.

topic: gradient descent on a loss landscape
prompt: Write a lyrical description of a neural network learning, imagining training as a blindfolded traveler descending a vast mountain range at night, feeling for the slope underfoot in search of a valley of low error.
Explain why the titan arum, or corpse flower, heats itself up and smells of rotting flesh when it blooms, and which pollinators it is trying to fool.
Explain Wittgenstein's idea of family resemblance by asking what board games, ball games, card games and solitaire actually have in common, and why many of our concepts lack crisp definitions.
Describe the moment in 1963 when Stanisław Ulam, doodling through a dull lecture, wrote the whole numbers in a square spiral and saw the primes gather along mysterious diagonal lines.
Write a haunting, reflective passage about Kafka's parable of the man who waits his whole life before the open door of the Law, only to learn at the very end that the door was meant for him alone.

Explain the diamond-water paradox, why water, essential to life, is cheap while diamonds are expensive, and how the idea of marginal utility finally resolved the puzzle, as if speaking to someone holding a glass of water in one hand and a diamond ring in the other.

Argue whether a handwritten letter carries something that no email or text message ever can, considering the ink, the handwriting, the slowness of the post and the fact that it can sit in a drawer for fifty years.
Explain why killer whales are among the very few animals that go through menopause, and how post-reproductive grandmothers lead their pods to salmon in lean years.

Explain the Alcubierre warp drive, a solution of Einstein's equations in which a ship rides a bubble of contracted space ahead and expanded space behind, and the exotic obstacles that keep it in the realm of speculation.

Explain what a Bose–Einstein condensate is, using the image of a crowd of individual singers merging into one perfectly unified choir to describe how atoms cooled near absolute zero begin to behave as a single quantum wave.

Describe the twelve seconds of the Wright brothers' first powered flight on the cold, windy dunes near Kitty Hawk in December 1903, as seen by one of the handful of local men who happened to witness it.

Explain modular arithmetic using the face of a clock, showing how this wrap-around way of counting underlies everything from working out the day of the week to the check digit printed on a book's barcode.

topic: Birth of the Monte Carlo method
prompt: Explain how the Monte Carlo method was born when Stanisław Ulam, convalescing from illness and playing solitaire, wondered whether he could estimate his odds of winning simply by playing many random games, and how the idea spread from there.

Explain to a frustrated commuter how Braess's paradox means that adding a new road to a congested network can make everyone's journey slower, and why removing a highway in Seoul did not cause traffic chaos.
Write a short story in which a reindeer herder in the Siberian taiga witnesses the Tunguska explosion on the morning of June 30, 1908.

Write a lyrical passage about the so-called 52-hertz whale, whose song is pitched higher than that of any known whale, imagining it calling across the Pacific for decades in a voice no other whale seems to answer.

Explain the grandfather paradox of time travel, imagining a traveler who journeys back to stop their grandparents from ever meeting, and the main escape routes proposed, from self-consistent timelines to branching universes.

topic: a message in a bottle's voyage
prompt: Describe the long, drifting voyage of a message in a bottle tossed from a ship's deck, carried by ocean currents for decades before washing up on a distant beach to be read by someone not yet born when it was written.
Write a lyrical description of a whale fall, the slow, decades-long feast that unfolds on the seafloor after a whale's body sinks into the deep.
Explain loss aversion and Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, beginning with why most people refuse a coin flip that would win them $150 on heads but cost them $100 on tails.

topic: Keynes's beauty contest and guessing games
prompt: Explain Keynes's 'beauty contest' analogy for financial markets, together with the 'guess two-thirds of the average' game that shows how investors end up trying to predict what others will predict.
Explain Robert Nozick's utility monster, a creature that gains vastly more pleasure from every resource than anyone else could, and why it is meant to embarrass simple versions of utilitarianism.

Explain Gauss's Theorema Egregium, his 'remarkable theorem' about curvature, using the trick of folding a floppy pizza slice into a U-shape so its tip doesn't droop, and show why it also means every flat map of the Earth must distort something.
